tamil:
கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி யொருவற்கு
மாடல்ல மற்றை யவை.
transliteration:
Kedil vizhuchchelvam kalvi oruvarku
Maadalla matraiyavai.
current_meaning: Learning is the one great treasure that can never be destroyed. Compared with it, all the other things people own are not real treasure at all.
elementary: Toys can break, money can be lost, and a house can burn down. What you have learned stays in your head, and no one can steal it. That is why Valluvar calls learning the best treasure of all.
university: The chapter ends with its thesis. Learning is கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம், 'imperishable, excellent wealth', and all other things are மாடு அல்ல, 'not wealth'. மாடு (maadu) is an old Tamil word for wealth that originally meant cattle, the earliest form of property, which gives the claim an archaic force. The argument works on two levels. Materially, learning cannot be stolen, taxed, destroyed or divided. Evaluatively, only learning deserves the name 'wealth' at all. Placing this conclusion in the Porul (Wealth) section is pointed, since Valluvar redefines the very wealth that section is about. The same claim appears almost word for word in the Sanskrit verse on vidyā-dhana, the wealth of knowledge that thieves cannot steal and kings cannot seize.

tamil:
அரங்கின்றி வட்டாடி யற்றே நிரம்பிய
நூலின்றிக் கோட்டி கொளல்.
transliteration:
Arangindri vattaadi yatre nirampiya
Noolindrik kotti kolal.
current_meaning: Speaking in a gathering of learned people without having fully learned your subject is like playing dice without a game board.
elementary: Imagine trying to play a board game when nobody has drawn the board. You can roll the dice, but none of your moves mean anything. This kural says that speaking in front of wise people when you haven’t really studied is exactly like that: lots of movement, no real game.
university: The image is precise: vattu (dice or game pieces) moved without an arangu (the ruled board or square) produce motion without rules, and therefore without meaning or result. Kotti (an assembly, a learned gathering) is the arena of debate, and nirampiya nool (complete, fully mastered texts) is the board that gives structure to every move. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as a warning to one who enters discussion with no framework of learning: his words, however energetic, have nothing to be scored against. The chapter thus opens by defining ignorance not as silence but as ungrounded speech. Across traditions, the parallel concern is the would-be teacher or debater who speaks confidently while ‘understanding neither what they say’ (1 Timothy), the Qur’anic ban on pursuing what one has no knowledge of, and Plato’s critique of the rhetorician who persuades without knowing.

tamil:
கல்லாதான் சொற்கா முறுதல் முலையிரண்டும்
இல்லாதாள் பெண்காமுற் றற்று.
transliteration:
Kallaadhaan sorkaa murudhal mulaiyirandum
Illaadhaal penkaamut rattru.
current_meaning: An uneducated person who wants to be admired as a speaker is like a woman with no breasts wishing to be desired as a woman.
elementary: Some people want everyone to listen to them, but they haven’t learned anything worth saying. Valluvar uses a blunt comparison from his own time: it’s like wanting to be admired for something you simply don’t have. The wish is there, but the thing that would make it come true is missing.
university: Sorkaamurudhal is a craving for speech — specifically the desire to be admired for eloquence in an assembly. Valluvar’s simile, jarring to modern ears, is built on the conventions of classical Tamil poetics, where breasts are a standard marker of feminine attractiveness; the point is structural rather than a comment on women: a desire whose necessary basis is absent is futile and invites ridicule. Learning is to speech what that physical attribute is to erotic appeal in the poetic code. Parallel traditions frame the same pathology as the fool who ‘hath no delight in understanding, but that his heart may discover itself’ (Proverbs 18:2), the Gita’s ‘men of small knowledge’ attached to flowery words, and the Dhammapada’s reminder that one is not wise because one speaks much. Modern readers may note the simile’s gendered framing as a product of its poetic era.

tamil:
கல்லா தவரும் நனிநல்லர் கற்றார்முன்
சொல்லா திருக்கப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Kallaa thavarum naninallar katraarmun
Sollaa thirukkap perin.
current_meaning: Even uneducated people will be thought of as very good, as long as they stay quiet in front of learned people.
elementary: If you don’t know much about a subject and you’re with experts, the smartest thing you can do is stay quiet and listen. People will actually think well of you for it. Talking would show what you don’t know; silence protects you and lets you learn.
university: The irony of nani nallar (‘exceedingly good’) is gentle but pointed: the unlearned person’s one available virtue is restraint. Parimelazhagar notes that silence both conceals the defect and avoids the harm of error. The verse inverts the previous kural — where the unlearned craved speech, here he is redeemed by abstaining from it. This is one of the most widely shared moral intuitions across cultures: Proverbs 17:28 (‘Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise’), Rabbi Akiva’s ‘a fence for wisdom is silence’, and the famous Sanskrit maxim of Bhartrhari that silence is the ornament of the unlearned in an assembly of scholars, which is an almost exact parallel. The Buddhist corpus adds the self-knowledge dimension: the fool who knows he is a fool is to that extent wise.

tamil:
கல்லாதான் ஒட்பம் கழியநன் றாயினும்
கொள்ளார் அறிவுடை யார்.
transliteration:
Kallaadhaan otpam kazhiyanan raayinum
Kollaar arivudai yaar.
current_meaning: Even if an uneducated person’s cleverness happens to be very good, wise people will not accept it as reliable.
elementary: Sometimes a person who never studied says something that sounds really smart. Wise people still don’t rely on it, because it’s a lucky hit, not something the person truly understands. Next time the same person may be completely wrong, and they won’t know the difference.
university: Otpam denotes native sharpness or cleverness; kazhiya nandru (‘exceedingly good’) concedes that it may even be impressive. Yet the wise (arivudaiyaar) do not ‘take’ (kollaar) it. Parimelazhagar’s explanation is epistemic: insight not grounded in learning is accidental and unreliable, so it cannot be built upon. This anticipates Plato’s distinction in the Meno between true opinion and knowledge — right opinions are valuable but ‘run away’ unless tied down by reasoning, like the statues of Daedalus. The kural is harder-edged than some traditions would allow: Pirkei Avot’s ‘look not at the vessel but at what is in it’ pushes the other way, and Cassandra’s myth dramatizes the tragedy of truth rejected because of its source. The accuracy notes below mark these as contrasts.

tamil:
கல்லா ஒருவன் தகைமை தலைப்பெய்து
சொல்லாடச் சோர்வு படும்.
transliteration:
Kallaa oruvan thagaimai thalaippeydhu
Sollaadach chorvu padum.
current_meaning: An uneducated person’s high opinion of themselves fades away as soon as they meet and talk with learned people.
elementary: Someone might think they’re very smart — until they start talking with people who have actually studied. Then, very quickly, it becomes clear how little they know, and their proud image falls apart.
university: Thagaimai is estimation or worth — here the self-estimation (or reputation) that the unlearned man carries; thalaippeydhu means ‘meeting, coming face to face’ (with the learned), and chorvu padum ‘will droop, fail’. The kural completes the logic of 402–403: the man who does not keep silent will be exposed in conversation. This is the drama of the Socratic elenchus, where confident interlocutors are shown in dialogue to lack what they claimed; Plato’s Phaedrus names the result ‘the show of wisdom without the reality’. The Mundaka and Katha Upanishads describe fools ‘wise in their own conceit’, and 1 Corinthians 8:2 compresses the diagnosis into a sentence. Dhammapada 63’s ‘fool who thinks himself wise’ is exactly the figure whose pride collapses here.

tamil:
உளரென்னும் மாத்திரையர் அல்லால் பயவாக்
களரனையர் கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Ularennum maaththiraiyar allaal payavaak
Kalaranaiyar kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: Uneducated people can only be said to exist. Beyond that, they are like salty land where nothing grows.
elementary: Some land is so salty that nothing grows on it, no matter how much rain falls. Valluvar says a person who never learns is like that land: they are there, alive, but nothing useful grows from them for themselves or anyone else.
university: Ularennum maaththiraiyar — ‘mere measure of existing’ — reduces the unlearned to bare presence. Kalar is saline or alkaline soil, proverbial in Tamil for barrenness; payavaa (‘unyielding’) insists on the absence of any fruit. The agricultural image makes learning the cultivation that turns land into field. Striking parallels exist: the Buddha’s Desana Sutta (SN 42.7) speaks of a field that is ‘salty’ and poor as the worst kind of soil; the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 79 compares recipients of knowledge to types of land, including barren land that neither holds water nor grows anything; Jeremiah 17:6 speaks of ‘a salt land and not inhabited’; Hesiod calls the man who neither thinks nor learns ‘unprofitable’; and Seneca’s ‘leisure without study is death… a tomb for the living man’ matches the Kural’s reduction of such a life to mere existence.

tamil:
நுண்மாண் நுழைபுலம் இல்லான் எழில்நலம்
மண்மாண் புனைபாவை யற்று.
transliteration:
Nunmaan nuzhaipulam illaan ezhilnalam
Manmaan punaipaavai yattru.
current_meaning: The good looks of a person who lacks deep, sharp understanding are like the beauty of a painted clay doll.
elementary: A clay doll can be painted to look wonderful, but there is nothing inside it — it can’t think. Valluvar says a good-looking person who hasn’t developed a sharp, curious mind is like that doll: nice to look at, but empty.
university: Nunmaan nuzhaipulam — ‘subtle, excellent, penetrating intellect’ — names the kind of understanding that learning produces, able to enter into (nuzhai) fine distinctions. Its absence makes ezhil nalam (beauty, handsomeness) into manmaan punai paavai: a clay figure elaborately decorated. The contrast is surface versus interior. Aesop’s fox, finding an actor’s mask, puts it memorably: a beautiful head, but no brains. Chanakya Niti 3.8 is an almost perfect Sanskrit parallel — beauty, youth and noble birth without learning are like scentless kimshuka flowers. The Qur’an describes those whose ‘forms please you’ as ‘pieces of wood propped up’, and Proverbs likens beauty without discretion to a gold ring in a swine’s snout.

tamil:
நல்லார்கண் பட்ட வறுமையின் இன்னாதே
கல்லார்கண் பட்ட திரு.
transliteration:
Nallaarkan patta varumaiyin innaadhe
Kallaarkan patta thiru.
current_meaning: Riches in the hands of uneducated people cause more misery than being poor causes for good people.
elementary: It’s sad when good, wise people are poor. But Valluvar says it’s even worse when foolish, unlearned people get lots of money — because they don’t know how to use it well, and they can cause harm to themselves and everyone around them.
university: Innaadhu (painful, harmful) is the operative comparative: both situations are bad, but thiru (wealth, fortune) in the hands of the unlearned (kallaar) is worse than poverty befalling the good (nallaar). Parimelazhagar explains that the learned poor still do good and are not diminished, whereas the unlearned rich use wealth for harm. The verse belongs to Porul’s concern with statecraft: resources without wisdom are a public danger. Plato’s Euthydemus argues that wealth and other ‘goods’ are good only under the guidance of wisdom and become greater evils under ignorance; the Dhammapada says riches ruin the foolish; the Qur’an forbids handing property to the weak-minded; and Ecclesiastes laments folly set in great dignity.

tamil:
மேற்பிறந்தா ராயினும் கல்லாதார் கீழ்ப்பிறந்தும்
கற்றார் அனைத்திலர் பாடு.
transliteration:
Merpirandhaa raayinum kallaadhaar keezhppirandhum
Katraar anaiththilar paadu.
current_meaning: Even if they are born into a high family, uneducated people are not worth as much as learned people born into a low one.
elementary: Some people think being born into an important family makes them better than others. Valluvar disagrees: a person from a humble family who has learned a lot is worth more than a high-born person who hasn’t learned anything. What you learn matters more than where you were born.
university: Merpirandhaar/keezhppirandhu (born high/born low) refers to the social hierarchy of birth in Valluvar’s world; paadu is dignity, worth or standing. The kural does not abolish hierarchy in theory but subordinates it to learning in practice, a notable move in a society structured by birth. The closest parallel is Mishnah Horayot 3:8: a mamzer who is a Torah scholar takes precedence over a High Priest who is ignorant. Buddhism’s Dhammapada 393 and the Vasala Sutta reject birth as the measure of a brahmin; the Upanishadic story of Satyakama Jabala shows a boy of unknown lineage accepted for his truthfulness; Plato’s myth of the metals places each child by the quality of soul, not parentage; and Ecclesiastes prefers a poor, wise youth to a foolish king.

tamil:
விலங்கொடு மக்கள் அனையர் இலங்குநூல்
கற்றாரோடு ஏனை யவர்.
transliteration:
Vilangodu makkal anaiyar ilangunool
Katraarodu enai yavar.
current_meaning: Next to people who have studied great books, uneducated people are like animals next to human beings.
elementary: Think of how different a person is from an animal. Valluvar says the difference between someone who has studied great books and someone who hasn’t is just as big. Learning is what makes us fully human.
university: The closing kural states the chapter’s thesis as a proportion: learned : unlearned :: humans : animals. Ilangu nool (‘shining, illustrious texts’) specifies that it is serious learning, not mere literacy, that marks the difference. The analogy draws on a long tradition, shared across cultures, that locates the distinctively human in reason and cultivated understanding. Bhartrhari’s Nitishataka 12 says one devoid of literature, music and art is a beast without tail and horns; Aristotle, asked how the educated differ from the uneducated, replied ‘as much as the living from the dead’; Psalm 49:20 compares the man in honour without understanding to the beasts that perish; the Qur’an (7:179) likens those who do not use their hearts to understand to livestock; and the Dhammapada’s man of little learning grows old ‘like a bull’.

tamil:
செல்வத்துள் செல்வம் செவிச்செல்வம் அச்செல்வம்
செல்வத்துள் எல்லாம் தலை.
transliteration:
Selvaththul selvam sevichchelvam achchelvam
Selvaththul ellaam thalai.
current_meaning: The riches you gain through your ears, by listening to wise people, are the treasure of all treasures. Of all riches, they come first.
elementary: People think of money, gold and houses as riches. Valluvar says the best treasure of all is what you gather by listening carefully to wise people. That kind of treasure goes into your mind, nobody can steal it, and it is worth more than any other.
university: The chapter opens with a deliberately repetitive line — செல்வம் occurs four times — which enacts its claim: among all the ‘wealths’, செவிச்செல்வம் (the wealth of the ear) is தலை, the head or chief. Placed in Porutpaal immediately after the chapters on learning (கல்வி) and its lack (கல்லாமை), this chapter supplements book-learning with கேள்வி, knowledge received orally from the learned — the dominant mode of transmitting knowledge in a largely oral culture. Parimelazhagar notes that hearing is especially valuable because it is available even to those who cannot study texts themselves, and because the ear receives the distilled result of another’s long learning. Calling it the ‘wealth’ of a treatise on polity is pointed: Valluvar ranks a cognitive possession above the material resources the rest of the book is about.

tamil:
செவிக்குணவு இல்லாத போழ்து சிறிது
வயிற்றுக்கும் ஈயப் படும்.
transliteration:
Sevikkunavu illaadha pozhdhu siridhu
Vayitrrukkum eeyap padum.
current_meaning: Only when there is nothing to feed the ears, no good teaching to listen to, should you give a little food to the stomach as well.
elementary: Imagine you are hungry but a wise teacher is speaking. Valluvar says: keep listening first! Feed your ears with good words, and only when there is nothing more to hear, give your tummy a little food.
university: The kural introduces the governing metaphor of the chapter — hearing as food (செவிக்கு உணவு) — and inverts the ordinary priority of bodily needs. The ‘உம்’ in வயிற்றுக்கும் (‘to the stomach too’) and the qualifier சிறிது (‘a little’) make the stomach a secondary and moderate claimant. Commentators read this not as a call to starve but as a hierarchy: instruction, once lost, may not recur, whereas food can be taken any time. The metaphor links this chapter to the Indian notion of the body as sustained by food and the mind by speech, and anticipates 413 (hearers as those who eat ‘ear-food’) and 420 (those who know only the mouth’s taste).

tamil:
செவியுணவின் கேள்வி உடையார் அவியுணவின்
ஆன்றாரோடு ஒப்பர் நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Seviyunavin kelvi udaiyaar aviyunavin
Aandraarodu oppar nilaththu.
current_meaning: People who have gained knowledge by listening, which is food for the ears, are equal on earth to the gods, who are fed by offerings in sacred fires.
elementary: In old times people offered food to the gods through a sacred fire. Valluvar says people who ‘eat’ wise words through their ears are like gods living on earth.
university: A carefully balanced pair of compounds: செவியுணவு (ear-food) is set against அவியுணவு (oblation-food, havis), so that ‘those who have hearing’ are matched with ‘the exalted ones who eat oblations’ — the devas. Parimelazhagar glosses ஆன்றார் as the celestials; நிலத்து (‘on earth’) marks the hearers as terrestrial counterparts of the gods. The logic continues the food metaphor of 412: just as the gods are sustained by subtle offerings rather than gross food, the learned are sustained by subtle instruction. The kural thus elevates the listener’s status, not merely the value of what is heard.

tamil:
கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் கேட்க அஃதொருவற்கு
ஒற்கத்தின் ஊற்றாந் துணை.
transliteration:
Katrilan aayinum ketka aqdhoruvarku
Orkaththin ootraandh thunai.
current_meaning: Even if you have not studied, listen to learned people. What you hear will hold you up like a walking stick when you are weak or in trouble.
elementary: Maybe you never got to go to school or read many books. That’s okay — just listen to wise people! What you hear will be like a walking stick that holds you up when life gets hard.
university: Here Valluvar extends the chapter’s value to the unlettered: கற்றிலன் ஆயினும் (‘though he has not learned’) concedes lack of formal study, but கேட்க is an imperative — listening remains possible for everyone. ஒற்கம் means weakness, falling, or distress; ஊற்று is a prop or support (the same word recurs in 415 as ஊற்றுக்கோல், ‘supporting staff’). The kural thus democratises knowledge in an oral society: hearing is a route to wisdom for those without access to texts, and its value is practical — it sustains one when fortune slips.

tamil:
இழுக்கல் உடையுழி ஊற்றுக்கோல் அற்றே
ஒழுக்கம் உடையார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Izhukkal udaiyuzhi ootrukkol atre
Ozhukkam udaiyaarvaaich chol.
current_meaning: The words of good people are like a walking stick for someone walking on slippery ground.
elementary: When you walk on a muddy, slippery path, a strong stick helps you not fall. Advice from good, honest people works the same way — it keeps you steady when life gets slippery.
university: The image is precise: இழுக்கல் is slipperiness (and by extension moral lapse), ஊற்றுக்கோல் a staff one leans on. The kural qualifies the source of hearing — not any speaker, but ஒழுக்கம் உடையார், those of upright conduct. Parimelazhagar emphasises that the words of the virtuous are trustworthy because their conduct confirms them, and that such words prevent a fall before it happens. The kural links the chapter to the earlier chapter on ஒழுக்கமுடைமை (conduct) and grounds the authority of what one hears in the moral character of the speaker.

tamil:
எனைத்தானும் நல்லவை கேட்க அனைத்தானும்
ஆன்ற பெருமை தரும்.
transliteration:
Enaiththaanum nallavai ketka anaiththaanum
Aandra perumai tharum.
current_meaning: Listen to good things, even if only a little. Even that little will bring you great honor.
elementary: You don’t have to listen to a huge lecture. Even hearing one small good idea is worth it, because even a little bit of goodness can make you a much better person.
university: The kural balances எனைத்தானும் (‘however little’) against அனைத்தானும் (‘to that very extent’), so that the benefit is proportionate to what is heard, yet always leads to ஆன்ற பெருமை — full, well-rounded greatness. Two conditions are embedded: the content must be நல்லவை (good things), and the act must be real listening. The couplet thus both encourages even small, occasional listening and implicitly warns against hearing what is not good — a selectivity that parallels many traditions’ counsel about what one lets into the ear.

tamil:
பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் பேதைமை சொல்லார் இழைத்துணர்ந்து
ஈண்டிய கேள்வி யவர்.
transliteration:
Pizhaiththunarndhum pedhaimai sollaar izhaiththunarndhu
Eendiya kelvi yavar.
current_meaning: People who have studied things closely and gathered much learning by listening will not say foolish things, even when they have understood something wrongly.
elementary: Everyone makes mistakes sometimes. But a person who has listened carefully to lots of wise people won’t say silly things even when they get confused, because all that good listening keeps them careful.
university: The paired participles பிழைத்துணர்ந்தும் (‘even having understood wrongly’) and இழைத்துணர்ந்து (‘having understood finely, as if threading’) frame the couplet. இழை (thread) suggests minute, careful examination; ஈண்டிய (‘amassed’) describes accumulated hearing. The kural is realistic: the learned may still err in perception, but their trained habit of mind prevents error from becoming foolish speech (பேதைமை). Hearing thus functions as a safeguard not of infallibility but of judgment.

tamil:
கேட்பினும் கேளாத் தகையவே கேள்வியால்
தோட்கப் படாத செவி.
transliteration:
Ketpinum kelaath thagaiyave kelviyaal
Thotkap padaadha sevi.
current_meaning: Ears that have not been pierced (opened up) by good teaching are no better than deaf ears, even though they hear sounds.
elementary: Your ears can hear noises all day, but if you never really listen to wise lessons, it’s almost like your ears don’t work. Real hearing means letting good lessons get inside.
university: The pun turns on கேள் (‘hear’): ears may கேட்பினும் (hear sounds) yet be கேளாத் தகைய (of the nature of not hearing, i.e., deaf) if not தோட்கப்பட்ட — ‘bored, pierced’ — by கேள்வி. The piercing alludes to the ear-boring ritual (and earrings) of Tamil custom: the true ornament and opening of the ear is instruction. The distinction between physiological hearing and receptive understanding is the heart of the kural and finds close echoes in prophetic and philosophical literature on ‘hearing without hearing’.

tamil:
நுணங்கிய கேள்வியர் அல்லார் வணங்கிய
வாயினர் ஆதல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Nunangiya kelviyar allaar vanangiya
Vaayinar aadhal aridhu.
current_meaning: People who have not gained fine, deep learning by listening find it hard to speak gently and politely.
elementary: People who have listened a lot to wise teachers usually speak kindly and humbly. People who haven’t listened much often find it hard to speak gently and politely.
university: Two adjectives govern the couplet: நுணங்கிய (fine, subtle) describes the quality of hearing, and வணங்கிய (bowed, humble) the quality of speech. The link is causal: refined hearing produces humility in speech, because the listener becomes aware of how much others know. Parimelazhagar reads வணங்கிய வாய் as speech that is modest and respectful. The kural thus connects the ear and the mouth: good speaking is an outcome of good listening — a theme echoed widely in wisdom literature that advises being quick to hear and slow to speak.

tamil:
செவியிற் சுவையுணரா வாயுணர்வின் மாக்கள்
அவியினும் வாழினும் என்.
transliteration:
Seviyir suvaiyunaraa vaayunarvin maakkal
Aviyinum vaazhinum en.
current_meaning: Some people know only the tastes of the mouth and not the tastes of the ear, like animals. What does it matter whether they live or die?
elementary: Some people only care about yummy food and never enjoy listening to wise words. Valluvar says, sharply, that such people live like animals — whether they live or die makes little difference to the world.
university: The closing kural returns to the food metaphor of 412–413 with a stinging contrast between செவியிற் சுவை (the ear’s taste) and வாயுணர்வு (mouth-knowledge, i.e., the palate). மாக்கள் denotes people without discernment — often glossed as ‘beast-like men’. The rhetorical question அவியினும் வாழினும் என் (‘whether they perish or live, what of it?’) declares their existence inconsequential. Some commentators take வாயுணர்வு as knowing only what one’s own mouth says, i.e., talkers who never listen; either way the chapter closes by denying full humanity to those who never cultivate hearing.

tamil:
அறிவற்றங் காக்குங் கருவி செறுவார்க்கும்
உள்ளழிக்க லாகா அரண்.
transliteration:
Arivatrang kaakkum karuvi seruvaarkkum
Ullazhikka laakaa aran.
current_meaning: Wisdom is a weapon that protects a person from ruin. It is also a fort inside them that enemies cannot break into or destroy.
elementary: Imagine having a shield and a castle that nobody can ever take away from you. Valluvar says good sense is exactly that. It protects you from making ruinous mistakes, and no enemy can break into it, because it lives inside you.
university: The couplet sets up the governing metaphor of the chapter: arivu is both karuvi (an instrument or weapon) and aran (a fortress). The word அற்றம் (atram) means destruction, ruin, or a vulnerable moment of exposure. Parimelazhagan reads arivu as the faculty that keeps a person from falling into ruin. The second line moves the fortress inward: உள் (ul) is 'inside', so this is a stronghold that attackers (செறுவார், 'those who hate') cannot tear down from within. Placing the chapter in Porutpal is significant. For a king, forts, armies, and treasuries are external defences that can be besieged or bribed away, while discernment cannot be captured. The pairing of 'weapon' and 'wall' covers both active and passive defence. Stoic thought makes the same move with Marcus Aurelius's 'inner citadel', and the Dhammapada's image of the mind fortified like a city is similar.

tamil:
சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா தீதொரீஇ
நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Sendra idaththaal selavidaa theethoreei
Nandrinpaal uyppa tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom means not letting the mind run wherever it wants. It keeps the mind away from evil and guides it toward good.
elementary: Your mind is a bit like a puppy that wants to run off in every direction. Wisdom is the leash. It stops the puppy from running into trouble and gently pulls it toward good things.
university: Here arivu is defined by its function over the mind (implied as the subject). சென்ற இடத்தால் செலவிடா means 'not letting it go wherever it goes'. தீது ஒரீஇ means 'removing it from evil', and நன்றின்பால் உய்ப்பது means 'leading it toward the good'. Three movements are involved: restraint, withdrawal, and redirection. Wisdom is therefore not only knowing the good but actively governing attention and desire. Parimelazhagan glosses the object as the mind driven by the five senses. The image matches Indian and Greek charioteer models of the psyche (Katha Upanishad, Plato's Phaedrus), where intelligence holds the reins of the senses. The Buddhist 'fletcher straightening the arrow' image is similar. The Kural is notably positive: wisdom does not simply suppress the mind, it 'leads' it (uyppathu) somewhere better.

tamil:
எப்பொருள் யார்யார்வாய்க் கேட்பினும் அப்பொருள்
மெய்ப்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Epporul yaaryaarvaaik ketpinum apporul
Meipporul kaanpa tharivu.
current_meaning: Whatever you hear, and whoever you hear it from, wisdom is finding the real truth of it.
elementary: Sometimes people believe something just because a famous or important person said it. Sometimes they ignore something true because someone they don't like said it. Valluvar says a wise person looks at what was said and asks, 'Is this actually true?', no matter who said it.
university: This is among the most frequently quoted Kurals, often cited as an early statement of critical thinking. The repetition யார்யார் ('whoever, whoever') stresses that the speaker's status, reputation, or hostility is irrelevant. The contrast between பொருள் (porul, the thing said or its surface content) and மெய்ப்பொருள் (meipporul, its true substance) separates what is asserted from what is real. Two errors are ruled out. One is deference to authority, accepting a claim because of who said it. The other is the ad hominem, rejecting it for the same reason. The Kural is less radical than modern empiricism, because it assumes the truth can be discerned through judgment. Still, its location of arivu in the evaluation of claims, not in the collecting of them, anticipates the Buddhist Kalama Sutta and Aristotle's 'truth above friends'. For a king in Porutpal, this is also advice about handling the reports of ministers, spies, and flatterers.

tamil:
எண்பொருள வாகச் செலச்சொல்லித் தான்பிறர்வாய்
நுண்பொருள் காண்ப தறிவு.
transliteration:
Enporula vaagach selachcholli thaanpirarvaai
Nunporul kaanpa tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom is speaking so that others easily understand you and remember what you said, and also catching the deeper meaning in what others say.
elementary: A wise person does two things with words. When they talk, they explain things so clearly that others understand easily. When they listen, they catch even the small, hidden points in what others are saying.
university: The couplet describes wisdom in communication as running in two directions. In speaking, எண்பொருள ஆக means 'so that the meaning is easy' and செலச் சொல்லி means 'speaking so that it goes in', that is, lodges in the listener. In listening, நுண்பொருள் காண்பது means 'seeing the subtle or fine meaning' in another's words. The contrast between எண் (easy, simple) and நுண் (subtle, fine) is deliberate. The wise person simplifies when giving and refines when receiving. This is a sophisticated account of communicative intelligence, close to what classical rhetoric called knowing one's audience (Plato's Phaedrus) and to hermeneutic charity in interpreting others. For rulers and ministers, the Porutpal setting, it is practical advice: make your orders clear, and read the unstated intentions of envoys and courtiers.

tamil:
உலகம் தழீஇய தொட்பம் மலர்தலும்
கூம்பலும் இல்ல தறிவு.
transliteration:
Ulagam thazheeiya thotpam malarthalum
Koombalum illa tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom is making friends with the great people of the world and keeping that friendship steady, not opening up like a flower at first and closing up later.
elementary: Some people are super friendly one day and cold the next, like a flower that opens in the morning and shuts at night. Valluvar says it is smart to make friends with good people. It is wise to stay the same kind friend every day, not hot one day and cold the next.
university: This is the most debated couplet in the chapter. ஒட்பம் (otpam) means excellence or sagacity, and உலகம் (ulagam, 'the world') is read by Parimelazhagan and most commentators as 'the great ones of the world' (uyarndhor). The first half therefore says that true excellence is to befriend the eminent. The second half uses a flower image: மலர்தல் (blooming, opening) and கூம்பல் (closing, as a flower does at dusk). Wisdom is keeping that friendship constant, neither over-effusive at the start nor withdrawing later. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi, Mu. Varadarasan) take the flower image more broadly as emotional equanimity in joy and sorrow. Both readings stress stability: arivu produces steadiness of disposition, especially in relationships. Aristotle's view that friendships of the good endure because goodness endures is a close parallel.

tamil:
எவ்வ துறைவது உலகம் உலகத்தோடு
அவ்வ துறைவ தறிவு.
transliteration:
Evva thuraivathu ulagam ulagaththodu
Avva thuraiva tharivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom is living in step with the world, behaving the way the best people in the world behave.
elementary: Every place has its own ways of doing things. A wise person notices how good people around them behave and fits in with them, instead of being odd or rude just to stand out.
university: The couplet turns on the parallel எவ்வது / அவ்வது ('in whatever way / in that way') and on the verb உறைதல் (to dwell or abide). Wisdom is to abide with the world in the way the world abides. As in 425, Parimelazhagan takes ulagam to mean the uyarndhor, the worthy or great of the world, not the crowd. The Kural is therefore not a call to conformity with the majority but to conduct in step with the accepted norms of the good. It still carries a real social insight: discernment includes reading context and custom and not acting eccentrically. This complements 423. There, wisdom judges claims independently; here, wisdom adapts one's conduct to the settled ways of good society. Parallels range from the Talmudic 'never deviate from local custom' to Paul's 'all things to all men' and Descartes's provisional maxim of following his country's customs.

tamil:
அறிவுடையார் ஆவ தறிவார் அறிவிலார்
அஃதறி கல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar aava tharivaar arivilaar
Aqdhari kallaa thavar.
current_meaning: Wise people know what is going to happen before it happens. Unwise people cannot know it.
elementary: If you see dark clouds, you know rain is coming and take an umbrella. A wise person is good at spotting what is going to happen next, while a foolish person gets caught by surprise every time.
university: This couplet defines wisdom and its lack by one criterion: foresight. ஆவது அறிவார் means 'they know what will come to be'. The second line mirrors it: the unwise are precisely those who cannot know that (அஃது அறிகல்லாதவர்). Commentators take ஆவது to mean the outcome or consequence of present actions and circumstances, not supernatural prophecy. Arivu here is predictive practical judgment, the ability to read causes forward to their effects. The Talmudic definition 'who is wise? One who sees what will be born' is almost a translation. Aristotle's phronesis includes deliberating well about what conduces to the good in the long run, and Hesiod's Prometheus (forethought) and Epimetheus (afterthought) personify the Kural's opposition. The couplet also prepares for 429, where foresight becomes protection.

tamil:
அஞ்சுவ தஞ்சாமை பேதைமை அஞ்சுவது
அஞ்சல் அறிவார் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Anjuva thanjaamai pethaimai anjuvathu
Anjal arivaar thozhil.
current_meaning: Not being afraid of what you should be afraid of is foolish. Being afraid of what you should be afraid of is the way of the wise.
elementary: Being brave does not mean being scared of nothing. A person who isn't afraid of touching a hot stove or running across a busy road is not brave, just foolish. Wise people are careful about the things that really are dangerous.
university: The couplet rests on the repeated verb அஞ்சு (to fear) in a tight chiastic pattern. அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சாமை ('not fearing the fearworthy') is பேதைமை (folly), and அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சல் ('fearing the fearworthy') is the practice (தொழில்) of the wise. Fear is treated not as a weakness to overcome but as an emotion to calibrate. Commentators apply it to wrongdoing, the anger of the powerful, and real dangers. This is almost exactly Aristotle's doctrine of courage as a mean: the brave person fears the right things in the right way, and fearlessness toward everything is rashness. The Dhammapada (317) and Proverbs (14:16) make the same point. In the Porutpal context, a king who fears nothing, not even enemies, public anger, or his own misdeeds, is a danger to the state.

tamil:
எதிரதாக் காக்கும் அறிவினார்க் கில்லை
அதிர வருவதோர் நோய்.
transliteration:
Ethirathaak kaakkum arivinaark killai
Athira varuvathor noi.
current_meaning: Wise people who prepare ahead for what is coming will never be hit by a disaster that makes them shake with fear.
elementary: If you know a storm is coming and you close the windows and bring in your toys, the storm can't really hurt you. Wise people prepare ahead of time, so when trouble comes it doesn't shake them.
university: Building on 427 (knowing what will come), this couplet adds action: எதிரதாக் காக்கும் means 'guarding against it as something ahead', that is, protecting oneself before a danger arrives. The result: இல்லை அதிர வருவதோர் நோய் ('there is no affliction that comes so as to make them shudder'). நோய் (noi) literally means disease but is used broadly for suffering or calamity, and அதிர (to shake or tremble) vividly describes the shock of being unprepared. The claim is not that the wise escape every misfortune but that nothing catches them off guard. This parallels the Stoic premeditatio malorum, the Panchatantra fable of the three fish, and Jesus's parable of the house built on rock. It links back to 421's image of arivu as a protective weapon.

tamil:
அறிவுடையார் எல்லா முடையார் அறிவிலார்
என்னுடைய ரேனும் இலர்.
transliteration:
Arivudaiyaar ellaa mudaiyaar arivilaar
Ennudaiya renum ilar.
current_meaning: People who have wisdom have everything. People without wisdom have nothing, whatever else they own.
elementary: Imagine someone with a huge pile of money but no sense. They would probably lose it all or use it badly. Someone with good sense can build up whatever they need. Valluvar says good sense is the one thing that counts as having everything.
university: The chapter ends with a sweeping summary built on the verb உடைமை (possession) that gives the chapter its title. அறிவுடையார் எல்லாம் உடையார் means 'the possessors of wisdom are possessors of all'. என்னுடையரேனும் இலர் means 'whatever they possess, they have nothing'. The point is that wisdom is the meta-possession that makes other possessions useful and secure. Without it, wealth, power, and allies are squandered or turned against their holder. It is striking that this appears in Porutpal, the book on wealth and statecraft: Valluvar ranks arivu above porul (wealth) itself. The Talmud's 'if you have acquired knowledge, what do you lack?' and Socrates's argument in the Euthydemus that wisdom is the only unconditional good are close parallels. Solomon's story, in which he chooses wisdom and receives everything else too, dramatises the same claim.

tamil:
செருக்குஞ் சினமும் சிறுமையும் இல்லார்
பெருக்கம் பெருமித நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Serukkunj chinamum sirumaiyum illaar
Perukkam perumitha neerththu.
current_meaning: People who are free from pride, anger and mean, petty ways will grow in success, and that success will be truly honored.
elementary: Some people get rich and then turn bossy, angry, and greedy for low pleasures. This kural says that when someone does well in life but stays humble, calm, and clean-minded, their success is the kind people truly respect.
university: The chapter opens by naming three faults (குற்றம்) a ruler must purge: செருக்கு (arrogance, the swelling of self that success breeds), சினம் (anger), and சிறுமை (literally ‘smallness’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss it as காமம், base lust or petty desire). The claim is conditional and political: பெருக்கம் (increase, prosperity) only becomes பெருமிதம் (dignity, honourable greatness) when these three are absent. Wealth and power are morally neutral amplifiers; what they amplify is character. The triadic diagnosis of pride, anger and desire as the roots of ruin is one of the most widely shared moral analyses across ancient traditions, from the Gita’s ‘demoniac’ qualities to the Mishnah’s list of things that ‘put a man out of the world’.

tamil:
இவறலும் மாண்பிறந்த மானமும் மாணா
உவகையும் ஏதம் இறைக்கு.
transliteration:
Ivaralum maanbirandha maanamum maanaa
Uvakaiyum yedham iraikku.
current_meaning: Being stingy, having pride about the wrong things, and taking joy in unworthy things are faults that harm a ruler.
elementary: A leader should not be stingy, should not be proud about the wrong things, and should not enjoy things that are low or harmful. This kural says those three habits are dangers for anyone in charge.
university: Valluvar adds a second triad specific to kingship (இறை, ‘the ruler’): இவறல் (miserliness, refusing to give what should be given), மாண்பு இறந்த மானம் (a sense of honour that has ‘died to excellence’, i.e. touchy pride over the wrong things; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as refusing to bow to the worthy out of pride of office), and மாணா உவகை (joy in what is unworthy). ஏதம் means harm or fault. Each is a perversion of a legitimate royal trait: prudence with wealth decays into avarice, dignity into vanity, and a king’s pleasures into indulgence. Miserliness returns in Kurals 437 and 438 as the gravest of all faults, so this couplet frames the chapter’s political core: a ruler’s private vices become public dangers.

tamil:
தினைத்துணையாங் குற்றம் வரினும் பனைத்துணையாக்
கொள்வர் பழிநாணு வார்.
transliteration:
Thinaiththunaiyaang kutram varinum panaiththunaiyaak
Kolvar pazhinaanu vaar.
current_meaning: People who fear shame treat even a fault as small as a millet seed as if it were as big as a palmyra palm (a very tall tree).
elementary: A millet seed is tiny, and a palm tree is huge. People who really care about doing right treat even a tiny mistake as if it were a giant one, so they fix it straight away instead of letting it grow.
university: The couplet turns on a vivid scale contrast between தினை (foxtail millet, among the smallest grains) and பனை (the palmyra palm, among the tallest trees). பழிநாணுவார், ‘those who are ashamed before blame’, are defined not by having no faults but by how they perceive them: they magnify their own errors in their own eyes. This is a moral psychology of vigilance. Shame (நாண்) works here as a protective faculty, the Tamil counterpart of Greek aidōs, that makes a small lapse feel intolerable before it can grow. The commentators divide on whether the sense is ‘they grieve over it as if it were huge’ (Puliyur Kesikan) or ‘they guard against it as if it were huge’ (Varadarasan, Karunanidhi); both readings share the principle of disproportionate self-scrutiny.

tamil:
குற்றமே காக்க பொருளாகக் குற்றமே
அற்றந் தரூஉம் பகை.
transliteration:
Kutrame kaakka porulaakak kutrame
Atran tharooum pakai.
current_meaning: Make guarding against faults your main goal, because faults are the very enemy that brings ruin.
elementary: We often worry about enemies outside us. This kural says the most dangerous enemy is a bad habit or mistake inside ourselves, because that is what can truly destroy us. So guarding against our own faults should be our main job.
university: The repetition of குற்றமே (‘fault itself’) in both lines is emphatic: the ēkāram singles out fault, not external foes, as the true enemy. பொருளாக can be read as ‘as the essential aim’ or, with a pun on பொருள் (wealth, the theme of the whole Porutpāl), ‘as though it were your treasure’: guarding against faults is to be protected like wealth. அற்றம் means ruin or destruction, and தரூஉம் is the prolonged (alapedai) form of தரும், ‘that which brings’. (The two digitised editions consulted print ‘த்ரூஉம்’, a typographical slip for தரூஉம்.) The political reading (Solomon Pappaiah) is that a state is destroyed less by invading armies than by the ruler’s own moral failings, which is the governing thesis of this chapter.

tamil:
வருமுன்னர்க் காவாதான் வாழ்க்கை எரிமுன்னர்
வைத்தூறு போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Varumunnark kaavaathaan vaazhkkai erimunnar
Vaiththooru polak kedum.
current_meaning: A person who does not guard against faults before they come will see their life destroyed, like a pile of straw in front of a fire.
elementary: Dry straw near a fire catches in a flash. This kural says that if you don’t protect yourself from mistakes before they happen, your life can go up in flames just as quickly.
university: The couplet is built on a pointed parallel of two முன்னர் (‘before’): வருமுன்னர் (before [the fault] comes) and எரிமுன்னர் (before the fire). Failure to act in the first ‘before’ puts one in the second. வைத்தூறு is a stack of straw (வைக்கோல் போர்), the most combustible of village materials, so the image stresses how sudden and total the ruin is once prevention has failed. This is the chapter’s case for preventive rather than corrective vigilance: once a fault has taken hold, correction may already be too late. The same principle appears in Valluvar’s wider political thought on foresight (compare Kural 442 in the next chapter, which praises counsellors who guard against troubles before they arrive).

tamil:
தன்குற்றம் நீக்கிப் பிறர்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
என்குற்ற மாகும் இறைக்கு.
transliteration:
Thankutram neekkip pirarkutrang kaankirpin
Enkutra maakum iraikku.
current_meaning: If a ruler first fixes his own faults and only then looks at the faults of others, what fault could ever harm him?
elementary: It is easy to spot what others are doing wrong. This kural says a good leader first looks at and fixes their own mistakes, and only then points out other people’s. A leader who does that has nothing to be blamed for.
university: This is the chapter’s central statement of self-scrutiny and its logic is sequential: தன்குற்றம் நீக்கி (having removed one’s own fault) comes before பிறர்குற்றம் காண் (seeing others’ faults). The verb காண்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to see’) implies that judging others rightly is a capacity earned by self-correction. The closing rhetorical question, என்குற்றம் ஆகும் இறைக்கு (‘what fault would there be for the king?’), expects the answer ‘none’. For a ruler whose office is to judge, this is the ethics of legitimate authority: the right to correct others rests on having corrected oneself. The couplet is the Tamil counterpart of the ‘mote and beam’ teaching and of the fable of the two wallets, but it is framed positively as a programme for governance rather than as a rebuke to hypocrisy.

tamil:
செயற்பால செய்யா திவறியான் செல்வம்
உயற்பால தன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seyarpaala seyyaa thivariyaan selvam
Uyarpaala thandrik kedum.
current_meaning: The riches of a stingy person who does not use them for what they should be used for will not last. They will be lost without doing any good.
elementary: Money is meant to be used for good things: helping people, caring for family, doing what is right. This kural says that if someone just sits on their money out of stinginess, it ends up wasted and lost anyway.
university: செயற்பால (‘things that ought to be done’) are the proper uses of wealth, which Valluvar elsewhere lists as giving, enjoyment and public works; இவறியான் is the one who clings (from இவறு, to hoard or be miserly). உயற்பாலது அன்றி means ‘without the quality of surviving / being saved’: hoarded wealth has no future. The argument is not only moral but practical: wealth that is not put to use is exposed to theft, confiscation and decay, and so the miser loses both the good he could have done and the wealth itself. The couplet returns to இவறல் from Kural 432 and prepares for 438’s verdict that miserliness is the worst of all faults.

tamil:
பற்றுள்ளம் என்னும் இவறன்மை எற்றுள்ளும்
எண்ணப் படுவதொன் றன்று.
transliteration:
Patrullam ennum ivaranmai etrullum
Ennap paduvathon randru.
current_meaning: Stinginess, the greedy grip that holds on to everything, is not counted along with other faults. It stands apart as worse than all of them.
elementary: This kural says that stinginess, a heart that grabs and won’t let go, is not just one bad habit on a list. It is in a class of its own, worse than all the others.
university: பற்றுள்ளம் (‘a clinging heart’) defines இவறன்மை (miserliness) as a disposition of attachment, not merely an act of not giving. The phrase எற்றுள்ளும் எண்ணப்படுவது ஒன்று அன்று (‘it is not a thing to be counted among any [faults]’) is deliberately ambiguous: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as ‘a separate fault that cannot be counted along with others’, and Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it as ‘the most terrible of all faults’. Either way it is the chapter’s climax on avarice, which has now appeared three times (432, 437, 438). The ruler-centred reading matters: a stingy king starves the gifts, rewards and public works on which loyalty and prosperity depend, so his avarice spreads into every other failure.

tamil:
வியவற்க எஞ்ஞான்றும் தன்னை நயவற்க
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
transliteration:
Viyavarka enjnaandrum thannai nayavarka
Nandri payavaa vinai.
current_meaning: Never, at any time, think too highly of yourself, and never want to do things that bring no good.
elementary: Being impressed with yourself makes you stop noticing your mistakes. This kural gives two simple rules: never be too proud of yourself, and don’t want to do things that don’t do any good.
university: Two prohibitions run in parallel: வியவற்க (do not wonder at, marvel at) with தன்னை (oneself), and நயவற்க (do not desire) with நன்றி பயவா வினை (deeds that yield no good). எஞ்ஞான்றும் (‘at any time’) makes the first absolute: even at the height of success, self-admiration is forbidden. The two are causally linked. Self-admiration blinds a person to their own faults, which undoes the self-scrutiny of Kural 436, and a self-admiring ruler is the one most easily drawn into vain, unprofitable projects. Solomon Pappaiah reads the second clause politically: a ruler should not want to do what does not benefit the country and its governance.

tamil:
காதல காதல் அறியாமை உய்க்கிற்பின்
ஏதில ஏதிலார் நூல்.
transliteration:
Kaadhala kaadhal ariyaamai uykkirpin
Edhila edhilaar nool.
current_meaning: If you can enjoy what you love without letting others know what you want, your enemies’ plans against you will fail.
elementary: If everyone knows exactly what you want most, people who wish you harm can use that to trick you. This kural says a wise leader keeps their wishes private, so enemies have nothing to use against them.
university: The couplet uses doubled words for effect: காதல காதல் (‘the things one loves, [and] one’s love’) and ஏதில ஏதிலார் (‘come to nothing, [the plans of] strangers/enemies’). ஏதிலார் means those unrelated or hostile, and நூல் here means their ‘science’ or stratagems, the craft by which they plot. உய்க்கிற்பின் (‘if one is able to experience/carry out’) makes the condition discretion, not renunciation: the ruler may pursue his desires, but must not let them be known. The logic ties the chapter together. A known weakness or appetite is itself a fault (குற்றம்) in the strategic sense, a gap in the armour. By closing the chapter this way, Valluvar moves from moral self-correction to political self-guarding: the ruler must hide from enemies the very desires that could be used to exploit him.

tamil:
அறனறிந்து மூத்த அறிவுடையார் கேண்மை
திறனறிந்து தேர்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu mootha arivudaiyaar kenmai
Thiranarindhu therndhu kolal.
current_meaning: Think carefully and find the right way to win the friendship of older, wise people who know dharma (the right way to live).
elementary: Some people know what is right and have learned a lot from long experience. This kural says: find people like that, think carefully about who they really are, and then work to make them your friends and helpers.
university: The chapter opens by fixing three qualifications for the ‘great’ (periyar): they know aram (virtue/duty), they are ‘mootha’ (ripened, whether in age or in understanding), and they possess arivu (knowledge). The verb structure is significant: ‘thiran arindhu’ (knowing the method) and ‘therndhu’ (having examined) both precede ‘kolal’ (taking). Friendship with the wise is not an accident of proximity but a deliberate, tested acquisition — a theme Valluvar develops later in the chapters on friendship (79–83). Parimelazhagar notes that this counsel is addressed first to the king, for whom advisers are an instrument of rule, but it generalises readily to anyone: one’s judgment is only as good as the judgment of those one keeps close.

tamil:
உற்றநோய் நீக்கி உறாஅமை முற்காக்கும்
பெற்றியார்ப் பேணிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Utranoi neekki uraaamai murkaakkum
Petriyaarp penik kolal.
current_meaning: Care for and keep close the people who can remove troubles that have already come and protect you from troubles still to come.
elementary: Some wise people can help you fix a problem you already have, and can also warn you about problems before they happen. This kural says: treat people like that with great care and keep them close.
university: ‘Noi’ literally means disease, but here it stands for any affliction — political, financial, or personal. The couplet distinguishes two functions of the wise counselor: the remedial (utra noi neekki, removing the affliction already suffered) and the preventive (uraamai murkaakkum, guarding beforehand against what has not yet arrived). The latter is the rarer gift, since it requires foresight. ‘Petriyaar’ denotes those who possess this capacity as a settled quality, and ‘penik kolal’ (cherishing and holding) implies that such people must be honored and maintained, not merely consulted when convenient.

tamil:
அரியவற்று ளெல்லாம் அரிதே பெரியாரைப்
பேணித் தமராக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Ariyavatru lellaam aridhe periyaaraip
Penith thamaraak kolal.
current_meaning: Of all rare things, the rarest is to respect great people and make them your own family.
elementary: Many things in life are hard to get. But this kural says the hardest and most precious thing of all is to have truly great people treat you like family, because you have honored and cared for them.
university: The superlative construction ‘ariyavatrul ellaam aridhe’ (rarest among all rare things) places the friendship of the great above wealth, armies, and territory, all of which are also ‘rare’ in the Porutpaal. The key word is ‘thamar’ — one’s own people, kin. Valluvar is not describing hiring an expert but transforming a great person into someone bound to you by affection and loyalty; ‘peni’ (having cherished) marks the reciprocity required. The rarity has two sources: the great are few, and they cannot be commanded — they must be won.

tamil:
தம்மிற் பெரியார் தமரா ஒழுகுதல்
வன்மையு ளெல்லாந் தலை.
transliteration:
Thammir periyaar thamaraa ozhukudhal
Vanmaiyu lellaan thalai.
current_meaning: Getting people who are greater than you to treat you as one of their own is the greatest of all strengths.
elementary: Being strong isn’t just about muscles or money. This kural says the best kind of strength is behaving in a way that makes people who are wiser and better than you want to be on your side.
university: ‘Thammil periyaar’ — those greater than oneself — is the pointed phrase. Rulers and the powerful typically surround themselves with inferiors who flatter; Valluvar calls instead for the humility to keep superiors as intimates. ‘Ozhukudhal’ (conducting oneself) makes this a matter of sustained behavior, not a single act. Calling it the chief of all ‘vanmai’ (strengths) reframes power itself: the strength that multiplies other strengths is the ability to attract and retain better minds.

tamil:
சூழ்வார்கண் ணாக ஒழுகலான் மன்னவன்
சூழ்வாரைச் சூழ்ந்து கொளல்.
transliteration:
Soozhvaarkan naaka ozhukalaan mannavan
Soozhvaaraich soozhndhu kolal.
current_meaning: A king must use his advisers as his eyes, so he should choose them only after thinking very carefully.
elementary: A king can’t see everything himself, so his advisers are like his eyes. If your eyes are bad, you can’t see clearly. So this kural says a leader must think very carefully before choosing advisers.
university: The couplet plays on the root ‘soozh’ (to deliberate, plan): ‘soozhvaar’ are those who deliberate, and the king must ‘soozhndhu’ (deliberate) in choosing them. The wordplay enacts the argument — deliberation is needed to choose the deliberators. ‘Kan aaka’ (as eyes) is the governing metaphor: a king perceives his realm largely through ministers’ reports and judgments, so their quality determines the accuracy of his vision. The later chapter on ministers (Amaichu, ch. 64) builds on this principle.

tamil:
தக்கா ரினத்தனாய்த் தானொழுக வல்லானைச்
செற்றார் செயக்கிடந்த தில்.
transliteration:
Thakkaa rinaththanaaith thaanozhuka vallaanaich
Chetraar seyakkidandha thil.
current_meaning: Enemies can do nothing against someone who is able to live as one of a group of good and worthy people.
elementary: If you stay close to good and wise people and act like one of them, your enemies will find there is nothing they can do to hurt you.
university: ‘Thakkaar inaththan’ — one who belongs to the fellowship of the worthy — moves from the friendship of individuals to membership in a circle. ‘Thaan ozhuka vallaan’ (one able himself to conduct himself so) implies that belonging requires one’s own discipline; the worthy will not keep company with the unworthy. The consequence is framed in the negative with total scope: ‘setraar seyak kidandhadhu il’ — there remains nothing for enemies to do. The protection is both practical (good advice closes vulnerabilities) and reputational (a ruler surrounded by the virtuous is hard to isolate).

tamil:
இடிக்குந் துணையாரை ஆள்வாரை யாரே
கெடுக்குந் தகைமை யவர்.
transliteration:
Idikkun thunaiyaarai aalvaarai yaare
Kedukkun thakaimai yavar.
current_meaning: Who can ruin people who keep friends brave enough to scold them when they are wrong?
elementary: A good friend will tell you when you are doing something wrong, even if it hurts to hear. This kural asks: if you keep friends like that close, who could ever bring you down?
university: ‘Idikkum’ means to strike or rebuke — Parimelazhagar glosses it as reproving the king when he errs. The couplet is a rhetorical question that assumes its answer: none. What protects the ruler is not deference but correction. The idea is especially pointed in a political treatise, since rulers are the persons least likely to hear criticism. ‘Aalvaar’ (those who rule / keep) suggests the king must actively maintain such critics in his service rather than merely tolerate them.

tamil:
இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத ஏமரா மன்னன்
கெடுப்பா ரிலானுங் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Idippaarai illaadha emaraa mannan
Keduppaa rilaanung kedum.
current_meaning: A king without anyone to scold and correct him has no protection, and he will be ruined even when no enemy is there to destroy him.
elementary: A king with nobody brave enough to tell him he’s wrong is like someone walking without looking. Even if no enemy attacks him, he will trip over his own mistakes and fall.
university: This is the converse of 447. ‘Emaraa’ means unprotected or unsafeguarded — the missing protection is precisely the rebuker. The striking phrase ‘keduppaar ilaanum kedum’ (perishes even without destroyers) locates the source of ruin inside: unchecked error compounds until it destroys. Valluvar thus anticipates a well-known insight of political thought — that autocrats surrounded by yes-men fall by their own misjudgments more often than by foreign conquest.

tamil:
முதலிலார்க் கூதிய மில்லை மதலையாஞ்
சார்பிலார்க் கில்லை நிலை.
transliteration:
Mudhalilaark kooodhiya millai madhalaiyaanj
Chaarbilaark killai nilai.
current_meaning: Just as there is no profit without money to start with, there is no steadiness for those without good people to support them.
elementary: You can’t earn money from a business if you have no money to start it. In the same way, you can’t stay steady and safe in life if you have no wise people to lean on.
university: An economic analogy fitting the Porutpaal: ‘mudhal’ (capital) is to ‘oodhiyam’ (profit) as ‘saarbu’ (support) is to ‘nilai’ (stability). ‘Madhalai’ is a prop or supporting beam — the support of the great is the load-bearing pillar of a leader’s position. The analogy implies that alliance with the worthy is not an optional extra but the principal on which all further returns are earned.

tamil:
பல்லார் பகைகொளலிற் பத்தடுத்த தீமைத்தே
நல்லார் தொடர்கை விடல்.
transliteration:
Pallaar pakaikolalir paththaduththa theemaiththe
Nallaar thodarkai vidal.
current_meaning: Losing the friendship of good people is ten times worse than making many enemies.
elementary: Having lots of enemies is bad. But this kural says losing the friendship of good people is ten times worse than that.
university: The chapter closes with a calculus: ‘paththu aduththa’ (ten times over) compares two harms. Enmity from many (pallaar) is external and can be countered; abandonment of good friends (nallaar thodarkai vidal) removes the very counsel and support by which enemies are countered — so it multiplies every other danger. The verb ‘vidal’ (letting go) places responsibility on the one who drops such friendships, whether through pride, neglect, or preference for flatterers.

tamil:
சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Sitrinam anjum perumai sirumaidhaan
Sutramaach soozhndhu vidum.
current_meaning: Great people are afraid of mixing with mean, small-minded people. But small-minded people pull such people close and treat them like their own family.
elementary: A truly great person is careful to stay away from petty, mean-spirited people, almost as if afraid of them. A small-minded person does the opposite: they happily pull those same people close and treat them like family.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining two temperaments through a single reaction: அஞ்சும் (‘fears, shrinks from’) versus சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும் (‘surrounds itself with them as kinsfolk’). The சிற்றினம் (‘small/mean kind’) are not necessarily criminals; commentators such as Parimelazhagar gloss them as the base-minded whose company slowly lowers one’s own standard. The chiasmus of பெருமை/சிறுமை (greatness/smallness) makes character a matter of affinity: we show what we are by whom we are comfortable with. This chapter is the deliberate counterweight to chapter 45 (பெரியாரைத் துணைக்கோடல, seeking the help of the great): what one should seek there, one should fear here.

tamil:
நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர்திரிந் தற்றாகும் மாந்தர்க்கு
இனத்தியல்ப தாகும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Nilaththiyalbaal neerthirindhu atraakum maandharkku
Inaththiyalba thaagum arivu.
current_meaning: Water changes its color and taste depending on the ground it flows over. In the same way, a person’s understanding takes on the nature of the people they spend time with.
elementary: Rain is pure when it falls, but it turns muddy, salty or sweet depending on the ground it runs over. Our minds work the same way: they pick up the colour and taste of the people we spend time with.
university: The simile works because rain is pure when it falls and only takes on colour, salt or sweetness from the ground (நிலத்தியல்பு) it touches. அறிவு here is not raw intelligence but practical understanding, the judgement a person brings to life. Valluvar’s claim is environmental: the mind is not a sealed container but something that absorbs from its surroundings. The next two couplets (453–454) sharpen this into a paradox: intelligence seems to belong to the mind but is actually supplied by one’s company.

tamil:
மனத்தானாம் மாந்தர்க் குணர்ச்சி இனத்தானாம்
இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்.
transliteration:
Manaththaanaam maandhark kunarchchi inaththaanaam
Innaan enappadunj chol.
current_meaning: Our power to understand things comes from our own mind. But how others judge us, saying “that is the kind of person they are,” comes from the friends we keep.
elementary: What you think and feel comes from inside you. But what other people say about you, like ‘he’s a good guy’ or ‘he’s trouble’, mostly depends on who your friends are.
university: The couplet sets inner and outer against each other: உணர்ச்சி (perception, awareness) arises from மனம் (mind), while reputation, இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல் (‘the word by which one is called such a man’), arises from இனம் (one’s group). This is a sociological observation: others cannot see into a person’s mind, so they judge by association. Valluvar does not call this judgement unfair. He treats it as a fact the prudent must reckon with, which is why the chapter sits in the Porul (polity) book rather than Aram. Together with 454 it forms a two-step argument: first reputation, then even inner wisdom, turns out to depend on one’s company.

tamil:
மனத்து ளதுபோலக் காட்டி ஒருவற்கு
இனத்துள தாகும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Manaththu ladhupolak kaatti oruvarku
Inaththu ladhaagum arivu.
current_meaning: A person’s good sense seems to live in their own mind. But it really comes from the group of people they spend time with.
elementary: We think our good sense is all our own. But look closely and much of it comes from the people around us: what they talk about, what they value, how they act.
university: காட்டி (‘making it appear’) is the key word. Valluvar grants that wisdom seems to live in one’s own mind, then corrects the appearance: it is actually இனத்துளது, lodged in one’s group. This is a strikingly early statement of what is now called distributed or socially embedded cognition: judgement is sustained by the conversations, norms and examples of a circle. It does not deny individual minds, which 453 affirmed, but it undercuts the pride of thinking oneself self-sufficient. The practical corollary, drawn out in 455–460, is that choosing one’s company is choosing one’s wisdom.

tamil:
மனந்தூய்மை செய்வினை தூய்மை இரண்டும்
இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்.
transliteration:
Mananthooimai seivinai thooimai irandum
Inanthooimai thoovaa varum.
current_meaning: A clean, pure mind and clean, pure actions both come from keeping company with good, pure people.
elementary: Having a clean heart and doing clean, honest things are both easier when the people around you are good. Good friends act like a support that keeps your thoughts and actions straight.
university: தூவா (‘support, prop, means’) is the pivot. Purity of mind (மனம்) and of action (செய்வினை), the two pillars of Aram, are made to depend on a third thing, purity of company (இனம்). This goes a step beyond 452’s simile: company is not just an influence on character but its enabling support. The triple repetition of தூய்மை holds the three purities together in one sound-chain, mirroring the argument. Parimelazhagar notes that although mind and deed seem to be individual possessions, they are sustained by one’s associates.

tamil:
மனந்தூயார்க் கெச்சம்நன் றாகும் இனந்தூயார்க்
கில்லைநன் றாகா வினை.
transliteration:
Mananthooyaark kechcham nanraagum inanthooyaark
Killai nanraakaa vinai.
current_meaning: People with pure minds leave behind a good name for those who come after them. People who keep pure company never do anything that is not good.
elementary: People with clean hearts leave good things behind them: good children, a good name. People whose friends are good never end up doing bad things, because their friends keep them on track.
university: எச்சம் (‘that which remains’) is read by Parimelazhagar as good progeny, and by others as the good name that outlives a person; both senses make purity of mind a matter of legacy. The second line is sharper: for those with pure company there is no deed that is not good (இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை). The double negative is emphatic. Good company does not merely encourage good action; it rules out bad action. The couplet divides the labour: the mind decides what one leaves behind, and company decides what one does.

tamil:
மனநலம் மன்னுயிர்க் காக்கம் இனநலம்
எல்லாப் புகழுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Mananalam mannuyirk kaakkam inanalam
Ellaap pugazhum tharum.
current_meaning: A good mind brings a person success and plenty. Good friends bring them every kind of praise and fame.
elementary: A good heart helps you do well in life. But good friends give you something extra: they help people everywhere know and respect you.
university: Here the parallelism moves from purity (தூய்மை) to goodness (நலம்), and the rewards from legacy to worldly outcomes: ஆக்கம் (prosperity, growth) from the mind, எல்லாப் புகழும் (every kind of fame) from company. The word எல்லா (‘all’) quietly ranks the second above the first. Prosperity may be private, but fame is by nature social and so depends on one’s circle. The couplet explains why reputation, discussed in 453, is not just vanity: in the Porul context of kingship and public life, renown is a resource, and it flows through association.

tamil:
மனநலம் நன்குடைய ராயினும் சான்றோர்க்கு
இனநலம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Mananalam nankudaiya raayinum saanrorkku
Inanalam emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: Even wise people who already have a very good mind find that good friends make them safer and stronger.
elementary: Even very good and wise people still need good friends. Good company works like a protective wall that keeps their goodness safe.
university: The concessive ஆயினும் (‘even though’) blocks the obvious objection: surely the already-good (சான்றோர்) do not need company? Valluvar replies that for them too, இனநலம் is ஏமாப்பு, security or fortification. The word suggests protection against the slow wearing-down of virtue by circumstance. Virtue, on this view, is not a fixed possession but a condition to be kept up, and company is part of the upkeep. The couplet guards against the moral self-sufficiency that 454 already undercut.

tamil:
மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமைமற் றஃதும்
இனநலத்தின் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Mananalaththin aakum marumaimat rahdhum
Inanalaththin emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: A good mind earns a happy life in the next world. Even that is made safe by keeping good company.
elementary: A good heart earns you happiness after this life. But good friends make that happiness even more certain by helping you stay good all the way through.
university: The previous couplet made good company a fortress for virtue in this life; this one extends the claim to மறுமை, the next world. Even the reward that seems most purely individual, earned by one’s own inner goodness (மனநலம்), is secured (ஏமாப்பு, repeated from 458) by one’s company. The மற்று… அஃதும் (‘and even that’) is emphatic. The pairing of 458 and 459 moves from this world to the next and leaves no domain where company does not matter.

tamil:
நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின்
அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்.
transliteration:
Nallinaththin oongum thunaiyillai theeyinaththin
Allar paduppadhooum il.
current_meaning: Nothing helps a person more than good friends, and nothing causes more pain and trouble than bad friends.
elementary: Good friends are the best help you can ever have. Bad friends are the worst trouble you can ever have. Nothing else comes close in either direction.
university: The chapter ends with a symmetrical superlative: nothing surpasses (ஊங்கு) good company as a support (துணை), and nothing causes as much suffering (அல்லல்) as bad company. The emphatic lengthening in படுப்பதூஉம் (an alapedai, or metrical vowel extension) stresses the second half, so the warning weighs more than the praise, in keeping with the chapter title. The couplet sums up the whole adhikaram and connects it to chapter 45: seek the great, avoid the small, because nothing else in life has as much power to help or harm.

tamil:
அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ஆகி வழிபயக்கும்
ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Azhivadhooum aavadhooum aaki vazhipayakkum,
Oodhiyamum soozhndhu seyal.
current_meaning: Before you do something, think about what you will lose, what you will gain, and what good will be left in the end. Only then begin.
elementary: Before you start something, ask three questions: What might I lose? What will I get? And after everything is added up, will it really be worth it? Only when you have thought about all three should you begin.
university: The opening couplet sets out a three-part calculus that governs the whole chapter: அழிவது (what is spent or destroyed at the outset — the cost), ஆவது (what comes into being — the gain), and வழிபயக்கும் ஊதியம் (the profit that results in due course — the net yield after costs are subtracted). The verb சூழ் (to deliberate, to survey all round) is the chapter’s keyword. Parimelazhagar reads the triad as capital outlay, return, and eventual surplus, which makes this one of the earliest cost-benefit formulations in world ethical literature. Placed in the Porul (polity) section, the kural is addressed first to rulers, but it is phrased generally enough to apply to any undertaking. The point is not to avoid risk but to see the whole ledger before committing.

tamil:
தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு
அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்.
transliteration:
Therindha inaththotu therndhennich cheyvaarkku,
Arumporul yaadhondrum il.
current_meaning: Nothing is too hard for people who first talk things over with carefully chosen advisers and then study the matter themselves before they act.
elementary: If you pick good, trustworthy friends, talk your plan over with them, and think it through yourself too, there is almost nothing you cannot get done.
university: The couplet joins two acts of discernment: தெரிந்த இனம் (a circle that has itself been tested and chosen — echoing the preceding chapters on seeking the help of the great and avoiding mean company, 44–46) and தேர்ந்து எண்ணி (having examined and reasoned). Counsel is only as good as the counsellors, so selection comes before consultation. The strong universal claim (‘no object is hard to attain’) is typical of Valluvar’s rhetoric, which states the ideal case to motivate the practice. The idea of the ruler’s council (mantra) was a central institution of classical Indian statecraft, and the Kural places it at the heart of deliberate action.

tamil:
ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை
ஊக்கார் அறிவுடை யார்.
transliteration:
Aakkam karudhi mudhalizhakkum seyvinai,
Ookkaar arivutai yaar.
current_meaning: Wise people will not take on a project that risks losing the money they already have just in the hope of making more later.
elementary: Smart people don’t risk everything they already have just because they hope to win something bigger. They protect what they have first.
university: The pairing ஆக்கம் (gain, increase) and முதல் (principal, capital) is commercial vocabulary and continues the ledger of 461. The verb ஊக்கார் (‘they will not be eager to / will not set about’) matters: Valluvar does not ban all risk, but says the wise will not be enthusiastic for ventures where the principal itself is at stake. This is a rule of prudence rather than timidity. It tells a ruler not to gamble the treasury or the kingdom’s security on speculative expansion. Later chapters praise energy and persistence (ஊக்கம், chapter 60), so the teaching is best read as ‘secure the base before seeking growth’.

tamil:
தெளிவி லதனைத் தொடங்கார் இளிவென்னும்
ஏதப்பாடு அஞ்சு பவர்.
transliteration:
Thelivi ladhanaith thotangaar ilivennum,
Edhappaatu anju bavar.
current_meaning: People who are afraid of being shamed by failure will not start anything whose plan and outcome are not clear to them.
elementary: People who care about their good name don’t start things they don’t fully understand, because failing halfway would make them look foolish.
university: தெளிவு (clarity, certainty) is the key concept: an undertaking is ‘தெளிவு இலது’ when its means, outcome, or one’s own ability to finish it are uncertain. The motive for restraint is இளிவு (humiliation, contempt), described as an ஏதப்பாடு (a harm or calamity). Valluvar treats reputation as a real asset of the ruler, and public failure as damage to it, not just wounded pride. Commentators differ slightly. Parimelazhagar stresses that the doubtful venture ends in ridicule, while modern commentators such as Kalaignar read it more broadly as avoiding dishonourable acts. Both readings rest on the same logic: foreseeable shame is itself a cost to include in deliberation.

tamil:
வகையறச் சூழா தெழுதல் பகைவரைப்
பாத்திப் படுப்பதோ ராறு.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarach choozhaa thezhudhal pakaivaraip,
Paaththip patuppadho raaru.
current_meaning: Rushing to fight enemies without planning every step is like preparing a field for them to grow strong in.
elementary: If you rush to fight someone without planning properly, you actually help them — like planting a seed in good soil and watering it so it grows bigger.
university: The metaphor is agricultural. பாத்தி is a prepared garden bed, and பாத்திப் படுத்தல் means settling a plant in such a bed so it takes root. A poorly planned attack does not just fail. It strengthens the enemy, who gains confidence, allies, and legitimacy from beating back a rash assault. வகையற (exhaustively, covering every category) points to the sixfold considerations of statecraft (strength, place, time, means, allies, and so on) that commentators read into the phrase. Pope renders it: ‘With plans not well matured to rise against your foe, / Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!’ It is the chapter’s one explicitly military couplet.

tamil:
செய்தக்க அல்ல செயக்கெடும் செய்தக்க
செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seydhakka alla seyak ketum seydhakka,
Seyyaamai yaanung ketum.
current_meaning: Doing what you should not do ruins you. Not doing what you should do ruins you just as much.
elementary: You can get into trouble in two ways: by doing something you shouldn’t, and by not doing something you should. Both can hurt you just as much.
university: The couplet is built on a chiastic repetition of செய்தக்க (‘what is fit to be done’). It balances sins of commission against sins of omission and treats both as equally ruinous (கெடும் … கெடும்). This keeps the chapter from turning into a counsel of timidity: deliberation is meant to discern the right action, and paralysis is as fatal as rashness. In a political reading, a ruler who neglects necessary measures (defence, justice, relief) falls as surely as one who pursues reckless ones. The same double structure is familiar from moral and legal traditions that separate positive duties from prohibitions.

tamil:
எண்ணித் துணிக கருமம் துணிந்தபின்
எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Ennith thunika karumam thunindhapin,
Ennuvam enbadhu izhukku.
current_meaning: Think it through first, and then decide what to do. Saying “we will think about it after we start” is shameful.
elementary: Do your thinking first, then make up your mind and go. Starting first and figuring it out later is a big mistake.
university: Probably the most-quoted couplet of the chapter. Its force comes from the sequence எண்ணி → துணிக (reflect → resolve) and the rejection of the reversed order துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் (‘having resolved, we shall reflect’). Two faults are excluded at once. One is beginning without deliberation. The other, implied, is wavering and reopening the question after committing, which dissipates resolve. துணிவு means both decision and courage, so the couplet unites prudence and boldness: deliberation belongs before action, and firmness belongs after decision. இழுக்கு (a slip, a blemish) casts the failure as a lapse of character, not merely of technique.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் பலர்நின்று
போற்றினும் பொத்துப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aatrin varundhaa varuththam palarnindru,
Potrinum poththup patum.
current_meaning: Work that is not done the right way will fail, even if many people stand by to help and protect it.
