elementary: If you work hard but in the wrong way, the project will fall apart — even if lots of people are trying to help hold it together.
university: ஆறு here means ‘way, proper method’. வருந்தா வருத்தம் (‘toil not toiled [in the right way]’) is effort poured out without a method. The verb போற்று (to guard, cherish, maintain) and பலர்நின்று (many standing together) anticipate the objection that sheer numbers or goodwill can make up for bad method. Valluvar denies it. பொத்துப் படும் means ‘it will spring a leak / be breached’, an image of a vessel or dam giving way. The couplet adds to the chapter’s argument: deliberation must choose not only whether to act but how, and a wrong method cannot be rescued by resources applied afterwards.

tamil:
நன்றாற்ற லுள்ளுந் தவறுண்டு அவரவர்
பண்பறிந் தாற்றாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Nandraatra lullun thavaruntu avaravar,
Panbarin dhaatraak katai.
current_meaning: Even when you try to do good, you can fail if you do not understand what each person is like and what suits them.
elementary: Even being kind can go wrong if you don’t understand the person you’re helping. What helps one person might upset another.
university: The couplet carries deliberation into benevolence itself. நன்று ஆற்றல் (doing good, conferring benefits) is normally praised without qualification, but Valluvar notes a தவறு (error, failure) that arises when one does not know அவரவர் பண்பு (the respective natures of each person). Parimelazhagar explains that benefits given to those whose nature does not suit them may be misused or may turn them hostile. For a ruler, rewards and favours are tools of policy and must fit their recipients. The reduplicated அவரவர் (‘each respectively’) insists on individual discernment rather than uniform treatment. Some editions spell the verb தவுறுண்டு; the standard reading is தவறுண்டு.

tamil:
எள்ளாத எண்ணிச் செயல்வேண்டும் தம்மொடு
கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு.
transliteration:
Ellaadha ennich cheyalventum thammotu,
Kollaadha kollaadhu ulagu.
current_meaning: Think carefully and do only things the world will not look down on. People do not accept actions that do not fit who you are and your place in life.
elementary: Before you act, ask: will good people respect this, and does it fit who I am? People won’t accept actions that don’t suit the person doing them.
university: The closing couplet adds a social test to the practical tests of the preceding kurals. எள்ளாத (‘what is not despised’) introduces public judgement, and the wordplay கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது (‘the world will not accept what is not accepted with oneself’) sets the criterion of fit. An action must suit the agent’s station, capacity and character (தம்மொடு). Parimelazhagar takes it that the world will not approve deeds out of keeping with one’s status, even when the deeds themselves are not bad. For a ruler, legitimacy depends on acting in ways subjects and peers can recognise as fitting. The chapter thus ends by setting individual calculation inside a community of judgement.

tamil:
வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும்
துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Vinaivaliyum thanvaliyum maatraan valiyum
Thunaivaliyum thookkich cheyal.
current_meaning: Before you act, compare four strengths: how much strength the job needs, how strong you are, how strong your opponent is, and how strong the helpers on each side are.
elementary: Before you start something big, stop and measure four things: how hard the job is, how strong you are, how strong the other side is, and who will help each of you. Only after weighing all four should you decide to go ahead.
university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a four-part audit: vinai-vali (the strength the undertaking requires), tan-vali (one’s own strength), maatraan-vali (the adversary’s) and thunai-vali (the strength of allies, which Parimelazhagar reads as the allies of both parties). The verb thookki, ‘weighing as on a balance’, governs all four terms, so action (seyal) is justified only by comparison. Assessing yourself alone is not enough. This is the centre of the Kural’s political realism, and it closely parallels Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra, whose ninth book opens with a chapter on knowing power, place, time, strength and weakness before any campaign. Prudence here is not timidity. It is what makes effective action possible.

tamil:
ஒல்வ தறிவது அறிந்ததன் கண்தங்கிச்
செல்வார்க்குச் செல்லாதது இல்.
transliteration:
Olvadhu arivadhu arindhadhan kan thangich
Chelvaarkkuch chellaadhadhu il.
current_meaning: Nothing is out of reach for people who know what they can do, learn what the job needs, and keep working steadily at it.
elementary: If you know what you’re able to do, learn everything you need for it, and then stick with it without giving up, there’s nothing you can’t reach.
university: This couplet turns the caution of 471 into confidence. It has three stages: olvadhu (discerning what is within one’s power), arivadhu (acquiring the knowledge the task needs) and thangi (settling into the work with steady application). The conclusion, chellaadhadhu il (‘there is nothing that will not go’ for such people), is not a claim to unlimited power. It is conditional: success without limit is promised only inside the field that honest self-assessment has marked out. Knowing your limits is exactly what lets you be effective within them. The verse also defends Valluvar’s realism against the charge of defeatism, since measuring your strength is meant to lead to action, not to paralysis.

tamil:
உடைத்தம் வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி
இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Udaiththam valiyariyaar ookkaththin ookki
Idaikkan murindhaar palar.
current_meaning: Many people did not know how strong they really were. They rushed into a task on excitement alone and broke down halfway.
elementary: Lots of people get very excited and jump into something big without checking whether they’re strong enough. Halfway through they run out of strength, and it all falls apart.
university: Udaiththam vali, ‘the strength they themselves possess’, is exactly what these people fail to know. Ookkam (zeal, drive) is praised elsewhere in the Kural, with a whole chapter on it (ch. 60, Ookkam Udaimai), so Valluvar is not condemning enthusiasm itself. He condemns enthusiasm cut loose from measurement. The verb murindhaar (‘they snapped’) suggests a branch or axle giving way under strain and looks ahead to the cart-axle image of 475. Palar (‘many’) gives the verse an empirical, historical tone: this is not a hypothetical but a pattern seen across many careers and kingdoms.

tamil:
அமைந்தாங் கொழுகான் அளவறியான் தன்னை
வியந்தான் விரைந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Amaindhaangu ozhugaan alavariyaan thannai
Viyandhaan viraindhu kedum.
current_meaning: A person who does not get along with others, does not know their own limits, and thinks too highly of themselves will soon be ruined.
elementary: Someone who won’t get along with others, doesn’t know how strong they really are, and keeps bragging about how great they are will fall very fast.
university: Three faults are linked here. The first is failing to fit one’s conduct to others (amaindhaangu ozhugaan, which commentators read as refusing to accommodate those around one, especially more powerful neighbours). The second is ignorance of one’s own measure (alavu ariyaan). The third is self-admiration (thannai viyandhaan). The first two are errors of judgement, and the third is the emotional state that keeps them going, because the self-admirer stops checking. Viraindhu (‘swiftly’) matters: pride does not merely lead to ruin eventually, it speeds it up.

tamil:
பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் அப்பண்டஞ்
சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்.
transliteration:
Peelipey saakaadum achchirum appandanj
Chaala miguththup peyin.
current_meaning: Even peacock feathers, which are very light, will break the axle of a cart if you pile on too many.
elementary: A peacock feather weighs almost nothing. But if you pile far too many onto a cart, even feathers will snap its axle. Lots of small things can add up to too much.
university: This is one of the Kural’s most famous images. The peacock feather (peeli) is the lightest of loads and the cart (saakaadu) a sturdy vehicle, yet when it is loaded chaala miguththu (‘in great excess’), the axle (achchu) breaks. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to kings: even weak enemies can overwhelm a strong ruler if they combine, so a king should not provoke many small foes at once. A broader reading applies it to any capacity. No strength is infinite, and sheer quantity can turn trifles into a fatal burden. The image anticipates the later proverb of the straw that breaks the camel’s back.

tamil:
நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார் அஃதிறந் தூக்கின்
உயிர்க்கிறுதி ஆகி விடும்.
transliteration:
Nunikkombar erinaar ahdhirandhu ookkin
Uyirkkirudhi aagi vidum.
current_meaning: A person who has climbed to the very tip of a tree branch and tries to climb even higher will fall and lose their life.
elementary: Imagine climbing a tree right out to the thinnest tip of a branch. If you try to go even further, the branch breaks and you fall. You need to know when you’ve gone as high as you safely can.
university: Nunikkombar, the thin end of a branch, marks the exact limit of what one’s strength, and the support one relies on, can bear. Commentators apply it to a ruler who has already stretched his power as far as it will go: any further push (ahdhu irandhu ookkin, ‘if he strives beyond it’) becomes fatal. The verse pairs with 475. There an external load exceeds capacity; here one’s own ambition exceeds the support beneath. The image is precise: the danger is greatest exactly when one is highest.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து ஈக அதுபொருள்
போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி.
transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu eega adhuporul
Potri vazhangu neri.
current_meaning: Know how much you have, and give in a sensible way. That is how you keep your money safe while still giving.
elementary: Being generous is good, but give in a way that fits what you actually have. That way you can keep helping people and still keep your household going.
university: Here the chapter turns from military to economic power, since for Valluvar wealth is also a form of vali. Aatrin means ‘in the proper way’, or in some readings ‘according to one’s capacity’. Alavu arindhu means knowing the measure of one’s wealth. The couplet reconciles two duties that could conflict: potri (preserving) and vazhangu (distributing). Measured giving is not stinginess. It is the method (neri) that makes generosity sustainable. Some web editions print aravarindhu here, but the standard Parimelazhagar text and most editions read alavarindhu, ‘knowing the measure’, which fits the chapter’s theme.

tamil:
ஆகாறு அளவிட்டி தாயினுங் கேடில்லை
போகாறு அகலாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Aagaaru alavittidhu aayinum kedillai
Pogaaru agalaak kadai.
current_meaning: It does no harm if the money coming in is small, as long as the money going out is not bigger.
elementary: It’s OK if you don’t earn much. What matters is that you don’t spend more than you earn. A small income with even smaller spending keeps you safe.
university: Aagaaru (the way wealth comes in) and pogaaru (the way it goes out) are channel metaphors, like the irrigation channels that feed and drain a village tank. Valluvar makes a ratio, not an absolute amount, the test of financial health. A narrow inflow (alavu ittidhu, ‘small in measure’) does no harm provided the outflow does not grow broader (agalaak kadai). The verse is often compared to Mr Micawber’s famous rule in Dickens, but it is well over a thousand years older. Within the chapter, it applies ‘knowledge of power’ to the household: one’s economic strength is the relation between inflow and outflow, not the size of either.

tamil:
அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் வாழ்க்கை உளபோல
இல்லாகித் தோன்றாக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Alavarindhu vaazhaadhaan vaazhkkai ulapola
Illaagith thondraak kedum.
current_meaning: A person who does not live within what they can afford may seem to be doing well, but their life will vanish and leave nothing behind.
elementary: Someone who spends as if they have more than they do might look rich for a while. But soon it all disappears, as if it had never been there.
university: The couplet diagnoses an illusion. Ula pola means ‘as if existing’: the spendthrift’s life looks abundant, but it illaagi (becomes nothing) and thondraak kedum (perishes without a trace, not even appearing afterwards). The phrase alavu arindhu vaazhaadhaan ties personal finance back to the chapter’s thesis: living well requires knowledge of one’s measure just as war does. The warning is less about spending itself than about the gap between appearance and substance. Wealth that is not measured is only apparent.

tamil:
உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புர வாண்மை
வளவரை வல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Ulavarai thookkaadha oppuravu aanmai
Valavarai vallaik kedum.
current_meaning: Giving away money without thinking about how much you really have will soon use up everything you own.
elementary: Helping others is wonderful, but if you give away more than you actually have, soon you’ll have nothing left, not even enough to keep helping.
university: Oppuravu is the civic virtue of beneficence to which Valluvar devotes chapter 22 (Oppuravu Arithal), where he says that even ruin incurred through beneficence is worth buying by selling oneself (220). Here he adds the prudential counterweight. Ulavarai thookkaadha describes beneficence that does not weigh (thookku, the same balance-verb as in 471) the extent of what one has, and it rapidly (vallai) destroys the limits of one’s wealth (valavarai). The chapter thus ends where it began, with weighing. Even virtue has to be measured against capacity if it is to last.

tamil:
பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை இகல்வெல்லும்
வேந்தர்க்கு வேண்டும் பொழுது.
transliteration:
Pakalvellum Kookaiyaik Kaakkai Ikalvellum
Vendharkku Ventum Pozhudhu.
current_meaning: In the daytime even a crow can beat the stronger owl. In the same way, a king who wants to beat his enemies must wait for the right time.
elementary: An owl is bigger and fiercer than a crow, but owls can hardly see in bright daylight. So in the daytime a crow can chase an owl away. If you pick the moment when you are at your best and the other side is at its weakest, even a small player can win.
university: The opening couplet grounds the chapter in natural observation. The kookai (owl) is stronger than the kaakkai (crow), but it is day-blind, so pakal (daytime) reverses their strength. Parimelazhagar draws the lesson for the vendhar (king): an ikal (hostile contest) is won not by strength alone but by the pozhudhu (hour) that suits one’s side. The image has a close Sanskrit parallel in the Panchatantra’s third book, the war of the crows and owls (Kākolūkīya), where the crows burn the owls’ cave by daylight. Both editions consulted (Thirukkural.net and Project Madurai) give the same text, apart from a sandhi spacing in ikalvellum.

tamil:
பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் திருவினைத்
தீராமை ஆர்க்குங் கயிறு.
transliteration:
Paruvaththotu Otta Ozhukal Thiruvinaith
Theeraamai Aarkkung Kayiru.
current_meaning: Acting at the right time is like a rope that ties good fortune down so it cannot slip away from you.
elementary: Farmers plant when the rains come, not whenever they like. If you do things at the right time, good luck stays with you as if tied by a rope. If you ignore the time, it wanders off.
university: Paruvam means season or ripe time, and otta ozhukal means conducting oneself so as to cling to it. The image in the second line is striking: thiru (Fortune, often personified as the goddess Lakshmi or Tirumakal) is fickle by nature, and timely action is the kayiru (rope) that aarkkum (binds) her so that she does not theeraamai, that is, depart. Parimelazhagar glosses paruvam as the time suited to the undertaking. He reads the couplet as a claim that wealth lasts only when action keeps pace with circumstance. Renaissance Europe has a close analogue in Machiavelli’s Fortuna, who favours the man whose conduct matches the times. The Tamil text is identical in both sources consulted.

tamil:
அருவினை யென்ப உளவோ கருவியான்
காலம் அறிந்து செயின்.
transliteration:
Aruvinai Yenpa Ulavo Karuviyaan
Kaalam Arindhu Seyin.
current_meaning: Is any task truly impossible if you do it with the right tools and at the right time?
elementary: Opening a tight jar is hard with bare hands. With the right tool and a little warm water it is easy. Most ‘impossible’ jobs become possible when you have the right tools and choose the right moment.
university: The couplet is a rhetorical question: aruvinai enpa ulavo, ‘are there things one could call hard deeds?’ The condition has two parts, karuviyaan (by means of instruments) and kaalam arindhu (knowing the time). Parimelazhagar takes karuvi to mean the resources of the state, such as army and treasury, together with the right methods. Neither timing without means nor means without timing is enough. The printed spelling ‘yenpa’ reflects sandhi with the preceding vowel; the word is enpa.

tamil:
ஞாலம் கருதினுங் கைகூடுங் காலம்
கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்.
transliteration:
Gnaalam Karudhinung Kaikootung Kaalam
Karudhi Itaththaar Seyin.
current_meaning: Even if you aim to win the whole world, you can get it, as long as you choose the right time and the right place to act.
elementary: A surfer can ride a huge wave, but only by paddling out at the right moment and at the right spot. Pick the right time and place, and even very big goals become reachable.
university: Gnaalam karudhinum means ‘even if one sets one’s mind on the earth’, that is, universal dominion, and kaikoodum means ‘it will come into one’s hand’. The condition joins kaalam karudhi (considering the time) with idaththaal seyin (acting by means of the place). This anticipates the next chapter, Idanarithal (Knowing the Place, Kurals 491–500). Parimelazhagar explains that idam here means a place of action favourable to oneself and difficult for the enemy. Time and place are treated as the two coordinates of successful action, as in the kāla and deśa of Sanskrit statecraft. Both sources give identical text; ‘karudhinung’ carries the nasal sandhi of karudhinum before k-.

tamil:
காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது
ஞாலம் கருது பவர்.
transliteration:
Kaalam Karudhi Iruppar Kalangaadhu
Gnaalam Karudhu Pavar.
current_meaning: People who want to win the world do not get upset or hasty. They wait calmly and watch for the right time.
elementary: A cat watching a mouse-hole sits very still and doesn’t get upset or jump too early. People with big goals are like that. They stay calm and wait for their chance.
university: The couplet picks up gnaalam karudhu (‘aiming at the world’) from the previous kural and shows the inner attitude that goes with it. Such people iruppar, ‘stay’ or ‘sit still’, and do so kalangaadhu, ‘without being agitated’. Parimelazhagar explains that they are not disturbed by the enemy’s present prosperity or by their own present setbacks, because they know that the favourable time will come. The virtue described is patience that is also watchfulness, an active waiting rather than inertia. The printed division ‘karudhu pavar’ is a metrical split of karudhupavar, and the two sources agree.

tamil:
ஊக்க முடையான் ஒடுக்கம் பொருதகர்
தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து.
transliteration:
Ookka Mutaiyaan Otukkam Porudhakar
Thaakkarkup Perun Thakaiththu.
current_meaning: When a strong, active person holds back for a while, it is like a fighting ram stepping back so it can charge harder.
elementary: When a ram wants to butt, it first walks backward a few steps, then rushes forward with great force. A strong person who waits quietly for a while is not giving up. They are getting ready to charge.
university: Ookkam means energy or zeal, and otukkam means drawing in, withdrawal or restraint. Porudhakar is a fighting ram (poru, ‘fight’, + thakar, ‘ram’), and thaakkal means butting or striking. Perum thakaiththu means ‘is of the nature of drawing back’, which Parimelazhagar reads as backing up to strike harder. The image reassures anyone who might misread the patient man’s restraint as weakness: his pause is how he gathers force. The same logic appears in the feigned retreats of military history and in Sun Tzu’s ‘coyness of a maiden’ followed by the rush of a hare. The printed ‘perun thakaiththu’ shows the nasal sandhi of perum before th-.

tamil:
பொள்ளென ஆங்கே புறம்வேரார் காலம்பார்த்து
உள்வேர்ப்பர் ஒள்ளி யவர்.
transliteration:
Pollena Aange Puramveraar Kaalampaarththu
Ulverppar Olli Yavar.
current_meaning: Wise people do not burst out in anger right away. They keep it inside and wait for the right time to act.
elementary: If someone is rude to you and you shout back at once, you may make things worse. A wise person stays calm on the outside, remembers what happened, and deals with it later at a better moment.
university: Pollena means suddenly or at once, and aange means right there. Puram veraar means ‘they do not sweat or seethe outwardly’, and ul verppar means ‘they seethe within’. Olliyavar are the bright or clear-minded. Parimelazhagar explains that when the wise are provoked by enemies, they do not show anger immediately, because doing so would warn the enemy. They hold it until kaalam paarththu, ‘watching for the time’. The couplet is about strategy, not ethical renunciation of anger: the feeling is kept and redirected, not dissolved. Commentators contrast it with Chapter 31 (Vekulaamai, ‘Not Being Angry’), where anger is to be given up entirely. The two sources agree; ‘olli yavar’ is a metrical split of olliyavar.

tamil:
செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை
காணின் கிழக்காம் தலை.
transliteration:
Serunaraik Kaanin Sumakka Iruvarai
Kaanin Kizhakkaam Thalai.
current_meaning: When you meet your enemies, put up with them and even show them respect. When their time to fall comes, they will fall headfirst.
elementary: Sometimes you have to put up with someone difficult who is stronger than you right now. If you stay patient, a time will come when they lose their power. Wait for that time instead of starting a fight you can’t win.
university: Serunar are enemies, and sumakka means ‘carry’ or ‘bear’. Parimelazhagar understands this as even showing them deference, carrying them ‘on one’s head’ as it were. Iruvarai is the limit or end-time, the point at which the enemy’s fortune has run out. Kizhakkaam thalai, ‘the head will turn downward’, comes from kizh (below). Parimelazhagar reads kizhakku here as keezh, ‘downward’, not the homonym meaning ‘east’. The advice is openly realpolitik: submit outwardly while weak and strike when the enemy’s time has come. It closely echoes Kanika’s counsel to Dhritarashtra in the Mahābhārata to carry the enemy on one’s shoulder and then smash him like a pot on a stone. Both sources give identical text.

tamil:
எய்தற் கரியது இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே
செய்தற் கரிய செயல்.
transliteration:
Eydhar Kariyadhu Iyaindhakkaal Annilaiye
Seydhar Kariya Seyal.
current_meaning: When a rare chance comes, grab it at once and do the thing that would be too hard to do at any other time.
elementary: Imagine a gate that opens only for a moment. If you run through right away, you get in. If you wait to think it over, it shuts. When a rare chance comes, use it straight away.
university: The couplet uses a chiasmus of ‘rare’ things: eydhar kariyadhu (what is hard to obtain, the rare opportunity) and seydhar kariya seyal (deeds hard to do). The link is annilaiye, ‘in that very state, at that very moment’. Iyaindhakkaal means ‘when it has come together’ or ‘when it has fallen into place’. Parimelazhagar stresses immediacy: the opportunity will not return, so the difficult act must be done while it lasts. The previous couplets counselled patience, and this one completes them by insisting that patience ends in decisive action. The Greek figure of Kairos, bald behind so that he cannot be grabbed once he has passed, is the classic Western emblem of the same idea. Text identical in both sources; ‘eydhar kariyadhu’ and ‘seydhar kariya’ are metrical splits of eydharkariyadhu and seydharkariya.

tamil:
கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து மற்றதன்
குத்தொக்க சீர்த்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Kokkokka Koompum Paruvaththu Matradhan
Kuththokka Seerththa Itaththu.
current_meaning: When the time is not right, wait quietly like a heron standing still. When the right moment comes, strike as fast and sure as the heron catches a fish.
elementary: Have you seen a heron fishing? It stands very still in the water for a long time. When a fish swims close, it stabs down in a flash. Be patient like the heron while you wait, and quick like the heron when your chance comes.
university: The chapter ends with a double simile built on the kokku (heron or crane). In the season of koompum, ‘folding in’ or ‘drawing oneself together’, one should kokku okka, ‘be like the heron’, standing motionless and seemingly asleep. When the time is seerththa, ‘excellent’ or ‘fitting’, one should be like its kuththu (stab). Parimelazhagar notes the pairing of stillness and sudden strike as the model of a king’s conduct toward enemies. The heron also appears in Manusmṛti 7.106 and in the Chāṇakya Nīti as a model of patient concentration, which suggests a shared South Asian stock image. Some texts, including the musical setting on Thirukkural.net, read ‘seerththa vidaththu’ with a glide consonant. The two editions consulted print ‘seerththa idaththu’.

tamil:
தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க முற்றும்
இடங்கண்ட பின்அல் லது.
transliteration:
Thodangarka evvinaiyum ellarka mutrum
Idanganda pinnal lathu.
current_meaning: Do not start a fight against an enemy, and do not look down on them, until you have found a place from which you can surround and defeat them.
elementary: Before a game of hide-and-seek, a smart player first looks around for the best hiding spot, and never thinks the seeker is too silly to find them. Valluvar says to do the same with any big task: find the right spot first, and never think the other side is weak.
university: The chapter opens the third member of the triad that runs through chapters 48 to 50: strength (vali), time (kaalam) and now place (idam). The key word is ‘mutrum idam’, a place from which one can encircle or besiege (mutruthal, to surround, to lay siege); Parimelazhagar and the modern word-glosses (for example thirukkural-thamizh.org) take it as the ground suited for investing the enemy. The two prohibitions are joined: ‘thodangarka’ (do not begin) and ‘ellarka’ (do not despise), so over-confidence and bad positioning are treated as a single error. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah take ‘ellarka’ as ‘do not scorn the enemy’, whereas Kalaignar reads it as ‘do not treat the undertaking itself as trivial’, a minor interpretive variant. Older printed texts give the sandhi form ‘தொடங்கற்க வெவ்வினையு மெள்ளற்க’, which modern editions split as ‘எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க’.

tamil:
முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கும் அரண்சேர்ந்தாம்
ஆக்கம் பலவுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Muranserntha moimbi navarkkum aransernthaam
Aakkam palavun tharum.
current_meaning: Even for people who are already strong in battle, fighting from a safe, well-protected place gives them many extra advantages.
elementary: Even the strongest kid in a snowball fight does better behind a snow wall. Being strong is good, but being strong and in a safe spot is much better.
university: ‘Muran’ means hostility or opposition and ‘moimbu’ means strength, so the first line describes people strong enough to take on an enemy. ‘Aran’ is the fortress, one of the six limbs of the state that later gets its own chapter (74, அரண்), and ‘aakkam’ is gain or prosperity. The ‘-um’ (even) in ‘navarkkum’ is the point: position adds to strength and is no substitute for the lack of it, which is why Parimelazhagar reads the verse as saying that even the mighty gain from a secure base. Modern glosses widen ‘aran’ to any safe place of operation, not only a walled fort (thirukkural-thamizh.org: ‘the place of action is safe’). Older printings show the sandhi ‘மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கு மரண்சேர்ந்தா மாக்கம்’.

tamil:
ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப இடனறிந்து
போற்றார்கண் போற்றிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Aatraarum aatri adupa idanarinthu
Potraarkan potrich cheyin.
current_meaning: Even weak people can become strong enough to win if they pick the right place, protect themselves well, and then act against their enemy.
elementary: A little cat on a high shelf can bat at a big dog that can’t reach it. The cat isn’t stronger, it just picked the right spot. Valluvar says even weak people can win if they choose their spot well and stay safe.
university: The verse turns on the wordplay ‘aatraarum aatri’: those who lack power (aatraar) come to have it (aatri) and destroy the enemy (adupa). ‘Potraar’ literally means ‘those who do not honour us’, a standard Kural word for enemies, and the next word ‘potri’ (having guarded, taken care) repeats the sound with the opposite meaning. Parimelazhagar reads ‘potri’ as the actor protecting himself, so the conditions for success are knowing the place and staying self-protected. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading; Kalaignar adds the idea of choosing the right place for the attack. The kural spells out what 492 implied: the right place can make up for missing strength, and not merely add to strength one already has.

tamil:
எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர் இடனறிந்து
துன்னியார் துன்னிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Enniyaar ennam izhappar idanarinthu
Thunniyaar thunnich cheyin.
current_meaning: Enemies who planned to beat you will lose their plans if you find the right place, stay close to it, and act from there.
elementary: A turtle pulled all the way into its shell makes the curious dog give up and walk away. When you are in the right place and stay there, the other side stops trying.
university: The verse repeats words in pairs: ‘enniyaar ennam’ (the plan of those who planned) and ‘thunniyaar thunni’ (those who reached the place, keeping close to it). ‘Thunnuthal’ means to approach, cling to or stay close; commentators read the second ‘thunni’ as keeping firmly to the chosen ground instead of drifting away from it. Parimelazhagar takes ‘enniyaar’ as enemies who expected to win, and ‘ennam izhappar’ as more than tactical defeat: they give up the intention itself. Kalaignar has the foe not even daring to think of victory, and Pulavar Kesikan takes ‘thunni’ as pressing the battle closely. Where 493 was about winning, this kural is about deterrence: the right position ends the contest before it begins.

tamil:
நெடும்புனலுள் வெல்லும் முதலை அடும்புனலின்
நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற.
transliteration:
Nedumpunalul vellum muthalai adumpunalin
Neengin athanaip pira.
current_meaning: In deep water a crocodile can beat other animals. But once it leaves the water, those same animals can beat it.
elementary: A fish is the best swimmer in the pond, but put it on the grass and it can hardly move. The crocodile is the same: a champion in the river, in trouble on dry land.
university: This is the chapter’s best-known image. ‘Nedumpunal’ is deep or wide water; ‘adum’ (kills, overcomes) is placed in the middle so that it can be read with either half. Parimelazhagar’s construction is: in deep water the crocodile defeats others; if it leaves the water, others (pira) kill it. The verse leaves out the verb of the second clause and borrows it from ‘adum’, typical Kural compression. The Sanskrit nīti tradition has the same image in a Pañcatantra verse (nakraḥ svasthānam āsādya gajendram api karṣati), where the crocodile in its own place drags even a lordly elephant but out of it is beaten by a dog. That suggests a shared South Asian stock of proverbs rather than direct borrowing.

tamil:
கடலோடா கால்வல் நெடுந்தேர் கடலோடும்
நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Kadalodaa kaalval nedunther kadalodum
Naavaayum odaa nilaththu.
current_meaning: A tall chariot with strong wheels cannot run on the sea, and a ship that sails the sea cannot run on land.
elementary: A bicycle is great on the road but useless in a swimming pool, and a boat is great in the pool but useless on the road. Every tool, and every person, has a place where it works best.
university: The kural uses a paired image: ‘kaal val nedunther’, the tall chariot with strong wheels (kaal, literally ‘leg’, here the wheel), and ‘naavaay’, the sea-going ship, a word related to Sanskrit nau and Latin navis, which shows early Tamil familiarity with maritime trade. The repeated verb ‘odaa’ (will not run) connects the two lines. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as an allegory for forces: land armies and naval forces each succeed only in their own element, so a king must match his forces to the terrain. Kalaignar makes it a general lesson that whoever chooses where to act must at least know that a chariot will not cross the sea. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss extends it to countries bordered by mountains, forests, sea or desert, each needing its own methods.

tamil:
அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா எஞ்சாமை
எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்.
transliteration:
Anjaamai allaal thunaivendaa enjaamai
Enni idaththaal seyin.
current_meaning: If you think everything through carefully and act from the right place, you need no other helper except your own courage.
elementary: If you have practised your speech, checked every page, and are standing in the right spot on stage, the only thing left to bring is courage. This kural says good planning and the right place leave you needing only a brave heart.
university: ‘Enjaamai enni’ means to think things through without remainder (enjuthal, to be left over), so planning comes first. ‘Idaththaal seyin’ means acting from, or by means of, the right place; the instrumental ‘-aal’ makes place the means of action. ‘Anjaamai allaal thunai vendaa’ says no ally is needed except fearlessness, so courage takes the place of all outside help. Parimelazhagar notes that thorough deliberation and the right ground remove the need for allies (thunai), which were discussed earlier under ‘Valiyarithal’ (ch. 48, thunaivali). Kalaignar’s gloss is about thorough method and leaves out place, a lighter reading than the traditional one.

tamil:
சிறுபடையான் செல்லிடம் சேரின் உறுபடையான்
ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Sirupadaiyaan sellidam serin urupadaiyaan
Ookkam azhinthu vidum.
current_meaning: If a leader with a small army stands on ground where it can fight well, a leader with a big army will lose his push and his advantage.
elementary: In a narrow hallway, one kid can block the way even if ten kids are trying to get through, because only one can squeeze in at a time. A small team in the right spot can stop a big team.
university: ‘Sellidam’ is the key word: ‘the place where one’s power prevails’ (sellu, to be current or valid, as with a coin that ‘passes’). Parimelazhagar reads it as ground favourable to the small army, where it can fight on its own terms. ‘Urupadaiyaan’ is the commander of a large or mighty army, and ‘ookkam’, his drive and self-confidence (the subject of chapter 60), is what gets destroyed. Solomon Pappaiah gives a different reading: when the large army goes after the small one into the place where the small one lies, the large army’s prestige is lost. The sense stays the same, but the grammar of ‘sellidam’ is read in another way.

tamil:
சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும் மாந்தர்
உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Sirainalanum seerum ilareninum maanthar
Urainilaththodu ottal arithu.
current_meaning: Even people with no strong fort and no great power are hard to beat if you attack them in their own homeland.
elementary: Even a small puppy barks bravely and is hard to chase out of its own house, because it knows every corner. People are hardest to beat at home.
university: ‘Sirai nalan’ is the excellence of an enclosure or defensive barrier (sirai also means a moat or a prison-wall), and ‘seer’ is any other kind of distinction or strength. ‘Urainilam’ is the land where people live, their home ground, and ‘ottal’ is read by Parimelazhagar as going there to engage them. The kural balances 492: there the advantage came from fortification, here it comes from simply being at home, with the home fighter’s knowledge of the land and motivation. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss makes the psychology explicit: the knowledge that one is defending one’s own place is itself a source of courage. The verse also works as a warning to the invader, who is always at a disadvantage on foreign ground.

tamil:
காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும் கண்ணஞ்சா
வேலாள் முகத்த களிறு.
transliteration:
Kaalaazh kalaril nariyadum kannanjaa
Velaal mukaththa kaliru.
current_meaning: A brave war elephant that can pierce spear-carrying soldiers with its tusks can be killed even by jackals when it gets stuck in deep mud.
elementary: A huge elephant is the strongest animal in the forest, but if it gets stuck in deep mud, even small animals can bother it and it can’t fight back. Being big and strong doesn’t help if you’re stuck in the wrong place.
university: The chapter closes with its strongest contrast. ‘Kaal aazh kalar’ is mire or saline swamp where legs sink; ‘kann anjaa’ is ‘unflinching of eye’, never afraid; ‘velaal mukaththa kaliru’ is the tusker that carries spear-bearing warriors (velaal) impaled on its tusks (mukam, the front), which Parimelazhagar explains as an elephant that has gored armed soldiers. The ‘nari’ is the jackal, the most contemptible of predators, so the verse sets the mightiest animal against the meanest. The old continuous text (thirukkural-thamizh.org) shows the sandhi ‘காலாழ் களரி னரியடுங் கண்ணஞ்சா வேலாண் முகத்த களிறு’, where ‘வேலாண்’ is ‘வேலாள்’ joined to ‘முகத்த’. The kural returns to 491’s warning: the greatest strength, put on the wrong ground, falls to the weakest enemy.

tamil:
அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின்
திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aramporul inbam uyirachcham naankin
Thirandherindhu thaerap padum.
current_meaning: Give a person an important job only after testing them in four ways: with doing right, with money, with pleasure, and with fear for their own life.
elementary: Before a coach makes someone team captain, she quietly watches: Do they play fair even when cheating would win? Do they share the snacks? Do they get distracted by fun and forget practice? Do they stay brave when things get scary? Only a kid who passes all four gets the armband.
university: The chapter title pairs தெரிதல் (examining, discerning) with தெளிதல் (arriving at clear confidence), and this opening couplet names the method: testing by the four ‘ways’ (திறம்) of அறம், பொருள், இன்பம் and உயிரச்சம். Parimelazhagar reads these as deliberate trials of the candidate’s mind, a reading made vivid by Solomon Pappaiah, who describes staged provocations on grounds of righteousness, money and a woman’s supposed affection, plus a feigned threat to life. This matches almost point for point Kautilya’s four upadhās (religious, monetary, love and fear allurements) in Arthaśāstra 1.10, and commentators have long noted the correspondence. Kalaignar instead turns the tests into positive qualities (firm in dharma, honest in money, not infatuated by pleasure, unafraid for one’s life). Both web sources give the couplet identically; the final verb தேறப்படும் (‘is to be trusted’) sets the key root தேறு that recurs through the chapter.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து குற்றத்தின் நீங்கி வடுப்பரியும்
நாணுடையான் சுட்டே தெளிவு.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhu kutraththin neengi vaduppariyum
Naanudaiyaan sutte thelivu.
current_meaning: Trust a person who comes from a good family, has no faults, and is so afraid of shame that they guard their good name.
elementary: Think about who you would let hold the class pet over the weekend. You would pick the kid from a caring home, who does not break rules, and who would feel really bad if people thought they had been careless. Feeling embarrassed about doing wrong is actually a superpower that keeps people honest.
university: Three qualifications are stacked: birth in a good lineage (குடிப்பிறப்பு), freedom from faults (குற்றம்), and நாண், the moral shame that fears a வடு, literally a scar, meaning a stain on one’s reputation. சுட்டே தெளிவு means ‘confidence rests on the one so pointed out’. Varadarasan and Pappaiah read குடி as literal family background, while Kalaignar reverses the logic: one who is faultless and ashamed of wrongdoing is thereby shown to be truly ‘high-born’, a reading that plays down birth in favour of conduct. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first phrase as removing the faults of one’s birth-group. Both sources agree on the text; the idea of நாண் as a guard against wrongdoing returns at length in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை).

tamil:
அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார் கண்ணும் தெரியுங்கால்
இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு.
transliteration:
Ariyakatru aasatraar kannum theriyungaal
Inmai aridhe veliru.
current_meaning: Even among people who have studied hard books and seem to have no faults, if you look closely, it is rare to find one with no ignorance at all.
elementary: Even the smartest kid in class, the one who knows every dinosaur name, might not know how to tie their shoes. Nobody knows everything. So when you choose someone for a job, check carefully instead of assuming they are perfect.
university: The couplet tempers the previous two: even the learned (அரிய கற்று) and flawless (ஆசு அற்றார்) will, on examination (தெரியுங்கால்), rarely be found without வெளிறு. வெளிறு literally means ‘whiteness’ and is used of weak, pale timber, and commentators gloss it as அறியாமை (ignorance) or a hidden weak spot. The practical lesson is that selection is not a search for a perfect person but a realistic judgment, which sets up the weighing of strengths and faults in the next couplet (504). Varadarasan and Pappaiah stress that no one is wholly free of ignorance, while Kalaignar aims the point at reputation: even those praised as flawless cannot be assumed so without examination. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி அவற்றுள்
மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kunamnaadik kutramum naadi avatrul
Migainaadi mikka kolal.
current_meaning: Look at a person’s good points, then at their faults. See which side is bigger, and judge them by that.
elementary: Imagine a friend who sometimes forgets your birthday but always shares, always helps, and always tells the truth. If you put the good things on one side of a see-saw and the forgetful thing on the other, the good side sinks way down. That’s how the Kural says to judge people: by which side is heavier.
university: The verb நாடு (to seek, look into) occurs three times, giving a three-step procedure: examine குணம் (good qualities), then குற்றம் (faults), then மிகை (which is greater), and finally கொளல், ‘take’ the person according to what is மிக்க (predominant). Following 503’s point that no one is flawless, this is a rule of proportion rather than perfection. Pappaiah narrows it to appointment (choose by the excess of virtues), while Kalaignar keeps it general: a clear judgment about someone comes only after this weighing. Some commentators note the ambiguity of மிக்க கொளல்: judge the person by what predominates, or keep the one in whom virtues predominate; either way the method is the same. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
பெருமைக்கும் ஏனைச் சிறுமைக்கும் தத்தம்
கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்.
transliteration:
Perumaikkum aenaich chirumaikkum thaththam
Karumame kattalaik kal.
current_meaning: Whether a person is great or mean and small, their own actions are the test that shows it.
elementary: A jeweller checks whether a ring is real gold by rubbing it on a special black stone and looking at the streak. You can check whether someone is really kind the same way, by looking at what they actually do, not what they say or what they wear.
university: கட்டளைக் கல் is the goldsmith’s touchstone (உரைகல்): gold rubbed on it leaves a streak whose colour shows its purity. The couplet says that deeds (கருமம், from Sanskrit karma) are such a stone for both பெருமை (greatness) and சிறுமை (meanness), and the emphatic ஏ in கருமமே excludes other tests such as birth, wealth or eloquence. It completes the lesson of 502: family is a starting presumption, but conduct is the decisive proof. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads கட்டளைக் கல் as an inscribed ‘edict stone’ that guides conduct, but the touchstone reading of Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Pope (‘touchstone true’) is standard. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
அற்றாரைத் தேறுதல் ஓம்புக மற்றவர்
பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி.
transliteration:
Atraaraith thaerudhal ombuga matravar
Patrilar naanaar pazhi.
current_meaning: Do not trust people who have no family or community ties. With no one to answer to, they feel no shame about doing wrong.
elementary: Why do people usually behave well? Partly because they don’t want to let down their family, friends and neighbours. Someone who doesn’t care about anyone might not care if they get in trouble either. So the Kural says: be careful before trusting someone who has no one they care about.
university: அற்றார் means ‘those who are cut off’; the standard commentary (followed by Varadarasan, Pappaiah and Pope) takes it as those without kin (சுற்றம்), who are therefore பற்றிலர், without attachments, and so நாணார் பழி, unashamed of blame. The reasoning links back to 502: shame works through the people whose opinion one values, so someone with no such bonds has no brake. Kalaignar reads அற்றார் as the unprincipled (நெறியற்றவர்), and Sivayogi Sivakumar reverses the sense, reading it as a call to raise up those who have nothing, a reading at odds with the chapter’s context. ஓம்புக here means ‘guard against, avoid’. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்
பேதைமை எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kaadhanmai kandhaa arivariyaarth thaerudhal
Paedhaimai ellaan tharum.
current_meaning: Trusting people who do not have the knowledge they need, just because you like them, will lead to every kind of foolish mistake.
elementary: Your best friend is awesome, but if they’ve never baked anything, you wouldn’t make them in charge of the cake for the whole school fair just because you like them. Liking someone is not the same as them being good at the job.
university: காதன்மை கந்தா means ‘with affection as the post’: கந்து is the post or pillar to which something is tied, so affection becomes the only support of the choice. அறிவு அறியார், ‘those who do not know what should be known’, names the risk, and the result is பேதைமை எல்லாம், every kind of folly. Pappaiah reads it as the folly produced by favouritism in appointments, and Kalaignar adds that such choices bear only useless results. Varadarasan’s printed gloss says the chooser’s ‘ignorance will perish’, which appears to be a typographical slip given his other readings and Pope’s ‘the height of folly’. The text reads எல்லாந் தரும் (sandhi of எல்லாம் + தரும்) in both sources.

tamil:
தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான் வழிமுறை
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Thaeraan piranaith thelindhaan vazhimurai
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
current_meaning: Someone who trusts a stranger without checking them first brings endless trouble, even to their own children and grandchildren.
elementary: If a stranger at the park says, “Give me your house key and I’ll water your plants,” and you just hand it over, trouble could follow your whole family for a long time. Trust has to be earned before you give it.
university: தேரான் (‘without examining’) and பிறன் (‘another, an outsider’) define the fault, and தெளிந்தான் (‘he who trusted’) the one who commits it. The key phrase வழிமுறை is read by Varadarasan and Kalaignar as ‘those who come after him’, his descendants, so the harm outlives the one who made the mistake; Pope follows this (‘on all his race’). Pappaiah shifts பிறன் to someone indifferent to the nation’s interests, a modern political reading. The second line தீரா இடும்பை தரும் is repeated word for word in 510, framing the chapter’s last three couplets with the same warning. ytamizh prints the couplet without the final full stop; the words are otherwise identical in both sources.

tamil:
தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின்
தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Thaerarka yaaraiyum thaeraadhu thaerndhapin
Thaeruga thaerum porul.
current_meaning: Do not trust anyone without checking them first. After checking, trust them with the things they can be trusted with.
elementary: Before you lend your favourite bike, you watch how your cousin treats their own toys. Once you’ve seen they’re careful, you lend it without nagging them every five minutes. Check first, then really trust.
university: The couplet plays on two nearly identical roots: தேர் (to examine, choose) and தேறு (to trust, be confident). Almost every word is built on them, a characteristic Valluvar wordplay that makes the rule easy to remember: தேறற்க … தேராது (do not trust without examining), தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக (after examining, trust). The closing phrase தேறும் பொருள் is read in two ways: Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as trusting in what deserves trust, while the older commentary followed by Pope takes it as entrusting to each person the duties suited to what the test showed. Pappaiah adds the practical corollary that one should not doubt someone after appointing them, which leads into 510. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Thaeraan thelivum thelindhaankan aiyuravum
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
current_meaning: Trusting someone you have not checked, and doubting someone you checked and then trusted, both bring endless trouble.
elementary: There are two ways to mess up with friends. One is trusting someone you just met with a big secret. The other is having a friend who has always been loyal and still checking their bag every day. Both make life miserable. Check carefully once, then trust.
university: The closing couplet names two opposite errors: தேரான் தெளிவு, confidence without examination (the fault of 508), and தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு, suspicion toward someone already tested and trusted. Both produce தீரா இடும்பை, ‘unending affliction’, repeating word for word the second line of 508, so the chapter ends by balancing its warnings: examination is required, but once done it must be honoured. Suspicion of a proven servant damages morale, invites real disloyalty, and wastes the effort of testing, points modern commentators such as Pappaiah and Kalaignar make explicit in the setting of appointments. The next chapter (52, தெரிந்து வினையாடல்) goes on to how the trusted person should be employed. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி நலம்புரிந்த
தன்மையான் ஆளப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nanmaiyum theemaiyum naadi nalampurindha
Thanmaiyaan aalap padum.
current_meaning: Give the job to the person who weighs the good and the bad in a matter and then naturally chooses to do what is good.
elementary: Imagine picking a team captain. You don’t pick the kid who just does whatever pops into their head. You pick the one who stops, thinks “what could go right, what could go wrong?”, and then chooses the good way. That’s the kind of person you give a job to.
university: The chapter opens by naming the first qualification of a worthy agent: not raw talent but a settled disposition (தன்மை) that examines (நாடி) both benefit and harm and then inclines (புரிந்த) toward the good. Varadarasan and Kalaignar read it as a test of the candidate’s character, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as an instruction to the appointee himself — once entrusted with a task, weigh its good and ill and do only what is good. Both readings converge on judgment joined to moral preference: discernment without a love of the good produces a clever but dangerous servant, and good intentions without discernment produce a well-meaning bungler. The pairing anticipates Aristotle’s prohairesis (deliberate choice) and the Upanishadic distinction between the good (śreyas) and the merely pleasant (preyas).

tamil:
வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை
ஆராய்வான் செய்க வினை.
transliteration:
Vaari perukki valampaduththu utravai
Aaraaivaan seyga vinai.
current_meaning: Give the work to someone who can find more ways to bring money in, make it grow, and spot and fix the problems that come up.
elementary: Think of someone looking after a lemonade stand. A good manager finds more customers, makes the stand earn more, and spots problems early, like running out of cups, and fixes them. That’s the person who should run the stand.
university: Kural 512 defines administrative competence in three verbs: பெருக்கி (expand the வாரி, the channels of revenue), வளம்படுத்து (turn income into lasting prosperity), and உற்றவை ஆராய் (look into whatever befalls, i.e., foresee and remove obstacles). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all read உற்றவை as the hindrances that threaten wealth, so the ideal agent is productive and protective at once. The couplet is strikingly economic: Valluvar judges the officer by measurable growth, not by birth or favour. Kautilya’s Arthashastra sets out the same standard, promoting superintendents who raise revenue and keeping in permanent service those who increase it loyally.

tamil:
அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை இந்நான்கும்
நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு.
transliteration:
Anbarivu thetram avaavinmai innaankum
Nangudaiyaan katte thelivu.
current_meaning: You can safely trust a person who fully has these four things: loyal love, knowledge, clear and firm thinking, and freedom from greed.
elementary: If you’re choosing someone to hold the class piggy bank, you want four things: they care about the class, they’re smart, they make clear decisions, and they don’t want the money for themselves. A person with all four is safe to trust.
university: Kural 513 is a compact job specification: அன்பு (attachment or loyalty to the ruler and the enterprise), அறிவு (knowledge), தேற்றம் (clarity and decisiveness; Varadarasan glosses it as the power to decide without doubt, Kalaignar as capacity to act), and அவாவின்மை (freedom from covetousness). நன்குடையான் stresses that the four must be held fully and steadily, not occasionally. Freedom from greed comes last, as the safeguard that keeps loyalty, knowledge and decisiveness from being turned to private gain. Jethro’s advice to Moses in Exodus 18:21, choosing capable men of truth who hate unjust gain, is an almost exact counterpart.

tamil:
எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான்
வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்.
transliteration:
Enaivagaiyaan theriyak kannum vinaivagaiyaan
Veraagum maandhar palar.
current_meaning: Even after being tested and approved in every way, many people turn out to be different once they actually start doing the work.
elementary: Someone can do great in a practice game and then play very differently in the real match. Tests help, but you only really know a person once they’re doing the actual job.
university: Having spent chapter 51 on testing (தெரிந்து தெளிதல்), Valluvar now admits its limits: however thoroughly a man is examined (எனைவகையான் தேறிய), the nature of the work itself (வினைவகையான்) can change him. Parimelazhagar sees here the corrupting pressure of office, wealth and power, and Pappaiah reads it as simple underperformance against expectations. The practical lesson, developed in Kural 520, is that selection must be followed by continuing supervision. The saying of Bias preserved by Aristotle, “rule will show the man,” states the same insight: power reveals what screening could not.

tamil:
அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு அல்லால் வினைதான்
சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற் றன்று.
transliteration:
Arindhaatrich cheygirpaarku allaal vinaidhaan
Sirandhaanendru evarpaat randru.
current_meaning: Give a job only to someone who knows how to do it and can push through the hard parts to finish it. Never give it to someone just because you like or admire them.
elementary: If the school play needs someone to run the lights, you don’t pick your best friend just because you like them. You pick the kid who knows how the lights work and won’t give up when something goes wrong.
university: The couplet sets competence against favouritism. Its first line gives the positive standard: அறிந்து (knowing the method), ஆற்றி (enduring obstacles) and செய்கிற்பான் (able to carry the task through). Its second line rules out appointing someone because he is சிறந்தான், someone the ruler holds dear or considers excellent in a general way. Pope’s “specious fav’rite” and Pappaiah’s gloss “thinking him one of our own (party, clan)” bring out the anti-nepotism edge. Plato’s ship of state, where sailors who have never learned navigation clamour to steer, dramatises the same danger.

tamil:
செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு
எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Seyvaanai naadi vinainaadik kaalaththodu
Eydha unarndhu seyal.
current_meaning: First judge the person who will do the work, then judge the work itself, and then act when the time is right for both.
elementary: To bake a cake you need the right baker, the right recipe, and the right moment, so it’s ready when the party starts. Get all three right and it works.
university: Kural 516 sets out a three-part planning method: examine the doer (செய்வானை நாடி), examine the deed (வினைநாடி), and fit both to the proper time (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து). Pappaiah reads it as bringing agent and task together and then matching the pair to the moment. The couplet also draws on the earlier chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Plato’s specialisation principle, that things go best when each person does the one thing natural to him and does it at the right time, runs remarkably parallel.

tamil:
இதனை இதனால் இவன்முடிக்கும் என்றாய்ந்து
அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்.
transliteration:
Idhanai idhanaal ivanmudikkum endraaindhu
Adhanai avankan vidal.
current_meaning: Once you decide that “this person can do this job in this way,” hand the job over to them and leave it in their hands.
elementary: When your teacher knows you’re good at drawing and have the markers you need, she gives you the class poster to make and then lets you do it, without hovering over every line.
university: The couplet is built on demonstratives: இதனை (this task), இதனால் (by these means), இவன் (this man), and then அதனை அவன்கண் விடல் (leave that with him). Delegation follows a specific three-way match of task, resources and person; Varadarasan glosses இதனால் as “by this instrument” and Pappaiah as the manpower and money available. விடல் (to release) implies real handing over, not a nominal assignment followed by micromanagement. Jethro’s advice in Exodus 18, and the master in the parable of the talents who gives each servant a share “according to his several ability” and then departs, express the same trust.

tamil:
வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை அவனை
அதற்குரிய னாகச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Vinaikkurimai naadiya pindrai avanai
Adharkuriya naagach cheyal.
current_meaning: After finding out what work a person is good at, put them fully in charge of it and give them the power to do it.
elementary: If you find out your friend is the best goalkeeper, you don’t just let them try out. You make them the goalkeeper for real, with the gloves and everything.
university: The key word is உரிமை, suitability and also rightful ownership. Once fitness for a task (வினைக்குரிமை) has been established, the ruler must make the person its rightful holder (அதற்குரியனாக). Pappaiah stresses the second half: having appointed a man, let him exercise the powers of the post himself. The couplet thus balances Kural 517: 517 is about handing over, 518 about conferring the standing and authority that make the handover real. It is Valluvar’s closest statement of the specialisation principle, which Plato made the definition of justice and the Gita discussed in terms of svadharma.

tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மைவே றாக
நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு.
transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaiyudaiyaan kenmaive raaga
Ninaippaanai neengum thiru.
current_meaning: Good fortune leaves a ruler who wrongly doubts the loyalty of a worker who is truly devoted to the work.
elementary: Imagine a kid who works really hard on a group project and is friendly with the teacher, and the teacher starts thinking “he must be up to something.” If you treat your best helpers that way, you lose them, and everything goes wrong.
university: The couplet warns against a failure of trust after appointment. வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் is the man wholly absorbed in his assigned work; கேண்மை வேறாக நினைத்தல் is to read his familiarity or friendship with the ruler as something else, such as presumption or disloyalty. Pope renders it as failing to bear the informal friendly ways of such servants, and Pappaiah adds the courtly setting of slanderers who poison the ruler’s mind against capable officers. The penalty is that திரு (prosperity, the goddess of fortune) departs, because a ruler who drives away his best workers destroys his own wealth. Saul’s jealousy of David is the classic Hebrew example.

tamil:
நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான்
கோடாமை கோடா துலகு.
transliteration:
Naadorum naaduga mannan vinaiseyvaan
Kodaamai kodaa thulagu.
current_meaning: A king should check every day how his workers behave. As long as they do not go wrong, the country will not go wrong either.
elementary: A good coach checks on the team at every practice, not just once at the start of the season. If the players stay on track, the whole team does well.
university: The chapter closes by joining selection to supervision: நாடோறும் நாடுக, examine every day. The logic is causal: if the worker does not swerve (கோடாமை), the world, meaning the realm and its people, will not swerve (கோடாது). Most commentators read it as vigilance over officials, but Kalaignar reads கோடாமை as the worker’s heart not withering, so the king’s daily attention becomes care for the welfare of labour. Kautilya prescribes almost the same thing, that superintendents be examined daily because men are changeable, which gives the Kural a precise parallel in Indian statecraft.

tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமைபா ராட்டுதல்
சுற்றத்தார் கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Patratra kannum pazhaimaipaa raattudhal
Sutraththaar kanne ula.
current_meaning: Even when a man has lost everything he had, only his relatives still honor the old bond they shared with him.
elementary: When someone’s pockets are full, lots of people want to sit next to them at lunch. But if they lose everything, most of those people drift away. Your family is different: they still remember the good times and stay by your side. That is what makes family special.
university: The chapter title சுற்றம் தழால் means ‘embracing the circle of kin’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as the king holding his kinsmen close so that they never leave him, and he explains that it follows ‘Selection and Employment’ (Ch. 52) because, having spoken of those who do the king’s work, Valluvar now turns to the rest of his ‘surround’. In this opening couplet பற்று means wealth or support, so பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் is ‘even when all holdings are gone’; the concessive உம் implies that such a man is normally no longer honoured by anyone. Parimelazhagar reads பழைமை as the kindnesses the man once did for them in his days of plenty, and the emphatic ஏ in கண்ணே stresses that kin alone keep faith, since others cut ties the moment the wealth is gone. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all agree on the sense, and Karunanidhi turns it into a definition: those who show this loyalty are the true kin. Editions differ only in sandhi (உள / யுள) at the end of the second line.

tamil:
விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின் அருப்பறா
ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
ViruppaRaach chutram iyaiyin aruppaRaa
Aakkam palavum tharum.
current_meaning: If a man has relatives whose love never fails, they will bring him many kinds of good fortune that keep on growing.
elementary: Think of a garden where lots of people help water the plants. The plants keep growing new branches and flowers. A family that loves you all the time works like those helpers: with them around, good things keep sprouting in your life.
university: Parimelazhagar notes that விருப்பறா (‘whose affection never ceases’) is there to exclude kin who are secret enemies (உட்பகை), and that அருப்பறா qualifies ஆக்கம் to mean wealth that never stops putting out new shoots (அருப்பு, ‘sprouting’, which he glosses as கிளைத்தல், ‘branching’). This separates it from wealth that grows only by its owner’s own effort. He explains the conditional இயையின் (‘if one should obtain’) as a sign of how rare such kin are, and reads பலவும் (‘all the many’) as pointing to the six limbs of the state (army, subjects, treasury, ministers, allies and fortress), which keep growing because many hands tend them together. The couplet sets out the economic logic of the chapter: kin are the root of expanding prosperity. The text is stable, and the Tamil commentators agree on the meaning.

tamil:
அளவளா வில்லாதான் வாழ்க்கை குளவளாக்
கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Alavalaa villaadhaan vaazhkkai kulavalaak
Kotindri neernirain thatru.
current_meaning: A man who does not share his heart with his relatives is like a big pond with no banks: whatever water comes in just flows away.
elementary: Imagine pouring water into a pond with no edges. The water spreads out and disappears, and the pond never stays full. A person who keeps away from family is like that pond: good things come, but with no one around to help hold on to them, they slip away.
university: The key word அளவளாவு means intimate mingling, literally ‘measuring together’. Parimelazhagar explains that heart-union grows out of exchanging one’s own measure with another’s, so the word stands by metonymy for close intimacy with kin, and ‘with kin’ is supplied from the chapter heading. குளவளா is the broad expanse of a tank and கோடு is its bank. For Parimelazhagar வாழ்க்கை here stands for the wealth that sustains life, and his point is that without kin to ‘hold’ it, a man’s wealth drains outward just as water spills from a tank that has no banks. He groups kurals 522-524 as showing kin to be the cause (ஏது), the fortress (அரண்) and the fruit (பயன்) of wealth, and this couplet shows kin as the fortress. Some printed texts divide the first word as அளவளாவு இல்லாதான், and thirukkural.net prints it with a space as அளவளா வில்லாதான்.

tamil:
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படஒழுகல் செல்வந்தான்
பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற பயன்.
transliteration:
Sutraththaal sutrap pataozhukal selvandhaan
Petraththaal petra payan.
current_meaning: The real reward of becoming rich is living in a way that keeps your relatives gathered around you.
elementary: Suppose you have a big box of snacks. If you eat them alone, it’s just snacks. If you share them, your cousins come and sit around you, laughing and talking. That circle of family is the real prize, not the snacks.
university: The couplet repeats sounds on purpose (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட, பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற) so that the verse itself seems to ‘surround’ its subject. Parimelazhagar glosses it as: the fruit a man gains from having gained wealth is to conduct himself, embracing his kin, so that he is encircled by them. He notes that in பெற்ற the final அ, and in அதனால் the particle அன், have dropped out for the sake of the rhyme. He explains that such conduct counts as the ‘fruit’ of wealth because it lets a king rule without enemies, and he treats it as the third term of the sequence cause–fortress–fruit (kurals 522-524). Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it the same way. The gloss attributed to Mu. Varadarasan for this kural on thirukkural.net actually belongs to kural 468 and is evidently misplaced there.

tamil:
கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் அடுக்கிய
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kotuththalum insolum aatrin atukkiya
Sutraththaal sutrap patum.
current_meaning: A man who gives freely and speaks kindly will be surrounded by relatives, circle after circle of them.
elementary: If you share your crayons and also say nice things to people, everyone wants to be near you. Then their brothers and sisters come too, and soon there’s a big happy circle around you. Sharing plus kind words is like a magnet for family.
university: Parimelazhagar notes that the verb ஆற்றின் (‘if one is able to accomplish’) stresses how hard it is to practise both virtues in due measure. He explains அடுக்கிய சுற்றம் as kin ‘stacked’ in succession: the kin of one’s kin, and then their kin, bound in a widening chain. He explicitly identifies the two means with the Sanskrit statecraft terms dāna (gift) and sāma (conciliation), the first two of the four upāyas, so this kural brings the Arthaśāstra toolkit into the domestic setting of kinship. Kurals 525-528, he says, set out the ‘means of embracing kin’. இன்சொல் (‘sweet speech’) links back to Chapter 10, இனியவை கூறல், and it anticipates the Buddhist saṅgahavatthu of giving and kind speech.

tamil:
பெருங்கொடையான் பேணான் வெகுளி அவனின்
மருங்குடையார் மாநிலத்து இல்.
transliteration:
Perungotaiyaan penaan vekuli avanin
Marungutaiyaar maanilaththu il.
current_meaning: No one on this wide earth has more relatives around him than a man who gives generously and does not hold on to anger.
elementary: Picture two kids. One shares a lot but gets angry and shouts all the time. The other shares and stays calm and kind. Everyone flocks to the second kid. Giving plus a calm heart brings the biggest family circle.
university: Parimelazhagar glosses பெருங்கொடை as ‘great liberality’ of a kind that never itself leads to want. He takes பேணான் வெகுளி (‘does not cherish anger’) to mean that the king does not indulge anger beyond measure, since he grants that a ruler may sometimes need to show it. மருங்கு (‘side’) here means kin (கிளை), so மருங்குடையார் are ‘those who have people at their side’. This kural adds a negative condition to the positive means of 525: generosity will not keep kin if it comes with an unpredictable temper, a point that looks ahead to Chapter 31 (வெகுளாமை) and to 306, where anger is said to burn the raft of one’s own people (இனம்). The text is stable, and all the main commentators agree.

tamil:
காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும்
அன்னநீ ரார்க்கே உள.
transliteration:
Kaakkai karavaa karaindhunnum aakkamum
Annanee raarkke ula.
current_meaning: A crow does not hide its food. It calls its family with a caw and eats with them. Good fortune comes only to people who are like that.
elementary: When a crow finds food, it doesn’t sneak off with it. It says ‘Caw! Caw!’ so its whole family comes to share. People who share like the crow end up with the most good things in life, because everyone sticks with them.
university: This is the best-known couplet of the chapter. Parimelazhagar explains that when crows find food they do not hide it (கரவா) but caw (கரைந்து) to summon their flock and eat together, and that the ‘prosperities’ (ஆக்கமும்) that come through kin belong only to those who have such a nature (அன்ன நீரார்). He lists those prosperities as freedom from enemies and great wealth. He reads the உம் in ஆக்கமும் as an ‘inclusive’ particle: such people gain not only virtue (அறம்) and pleasure (இன்பம்) but material wealth (பொருள்) as well. He defines the crow-like nature as arranging things so that kin enjoy everything one enjoys oneself. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi) take ஆக்கம் more broadly as ‘elevation’. The crow’s calling of its kin is proverbial in Tamil culture and is echoed in later didactic literature.

tamil:
பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்
அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Podhunokkaan vendhan varisaiyaa nokkin
Adhunokki vaazhvaar palar.
current_meaning: If a king does not treat everyone the same but gives each person the respect their worth deserves, many people will stay close to him because of it.
elementary: A good coach doesn’t give every player the same job. The fastest runner plays forward, and the one with the best hands becomes goalkeeper. When each person feels truly seen for what they’re good at, they all want to stay on the team.
university: The couplet contrasts பொது நோக்கு (‘common or uniform regard’) with வரிசை நோக்கு (‘regard according to rank or order’). Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை as each person’s own worth (தத்தம் தகுதி). He explains that uniform treatment is rejected because it drives away the superior, who feel slighted, while graded regard is prescribed because it keeps everyone loyal. This makes it a principle of proportional, not arithmetic, equality, very like Aristotle’s distributive justice. With this kural Parimelazhagar closes the four-verse unit (525-528) on the ‘means of embracing kin’. Karunanidhi’s modern gloss softens the hierarchy (‘all people are equal, but use each according to ability’), and Pappaiah places the kural explicitly within the ruler’s treatment of his kin.

tamil:
தமராகித் தற்றுறந்தார் சுற்றம் அமராமைக்
காரணம் இன்றி வரும்.
transliteration:
Thamaraakith thatrurandhaar sutram amaraamaik
Kaaranam indri varum.
current_meaning: Relatives who were once close but left because of some hurt will come back on their own once the cause of the fight is gone.
elementary: Suppose your cousin stopped coming over because you kept teasing him. If you stop teasing, he’ll start coming back all by himself. When you fix the reason someone left, the friendship often heals itself.
university: Parimelazhagar construes the couplet as: when those who were once one’s own (தமர்) have left because of some cause, their becoming kin again ‘comes’ (வரும்) of itself once that cause of discord (அமராமைக் காரணம்) no longer exists in oneself. He infers from the phrase that the cause really did exist before, and names it as the king’s own conduct, such as straying from the right path or doing things that displease. Because the kin were naturally affectionate and the estrangement was artificial, it ends when its cause ends; the ruler need not court them again, since they ‘return’ to their old nature. Pappaiah reads the kural in modern political terms, as members returning to a movement once the leader’s fault is gone. Karunanidhi reads it differently: those who left on some pretext come back once they see the pretext does not hold. Thirukkural.net prints தமராகிக் in the first word, but Parimelazhagar’s text on Wikisource and the standard editions read தமராகித், which is the reading adopted here.

tamil:
உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தானை வேந்தன்
இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Uzhaippirindhu kaaranaththin vandhaanai vendhan
Izhaiththirundhu ennik kolal.
current_meaning: When a relative who left the king for no reason comes back wanting something, the king should give what they need, but wait and judge them carefully before taking them back.
elementary: Imagine a teammate who quit for no reason and now wants to rejoin because he needs something. The captain can help him, but should watch how he behaves for a while before trusting him fully again. Welcome back, but with open eyes.
university: Parimelazhagar takes the bare உழைப் பிரிந்து (‘having left one’s side’) to imply that there was no reason for leaving, and காரணத்தின் வந்தானை as ‘one who came back because of some purpose’. He explains இழைத்திருந்து as ‘having done or supplied that purpose’: if the king does not meet the motive that brought the man back, he may leave again and join the enemy. He explains எண்ணிக் கொளல் as ‘accept him after examination’, because the man left without love and came back out of interest. Taken together with 529, Parimelazhagar sees two cases: the kinsman whom the king’s own fault drove away should be allowed to return freely, while the one who left without cause should be taken back only after scrutiny. Varadarasan similarly says the king should grant the help sought and then examine before re-admitting him, while Pappaiah reads இழைத்திருந்து as ‘waiting patiently’. Karunanidhi instead describes the man as one who left on a pretext and returned for a genuine reason.

tamil:
இறந்த வெகுளியின் தீதே சிறந்த
உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Irandha vekuliyin theedhe sirandha
Uvakai makizhchchiyir sorvu.
current_meaning: Becoming careless because you are carried away by great joy does more harm than even anger that has gone out of control.
elementary: Imagine a team that is winning a game by a lot. The players start celebrating early, stop paying attention, and the other team sneaks back and wins. Getting too excited and careless can hurt you even more than losing your temper, because you don't even notice the danger coming.
university: The chapter title பொச்சாவாமை is the negative verbal noun of பொச்சா- (‘to forget, to be negligent’; compare பொச்சாப்பு, ‘forgetfulness, heedlessness’). So it names a positive discipline of not forgetting, and because it sits in the Arasiyal (royal conduct) section, Parimelazhagar reads the whole chapter as advice to a king. In this couplet சோர்வு is the lapse or slackening born of சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சி, ‘the delight of surpassing joy’, and இறந்த வெகுளி is anger that has gone past all bounds. Parimelazhagar says that such joy comes from great wealth, great pleasure and great pride. He explains the comparison this way: measured anger is needed to crush enemies and punish the wicked, and even excessive anger may sometimes kill a foe, but forgetfulness born of joy kills only the person who has it, so it is the worse evil. Manakkudavar agrees on the sense but records another way to read the phrase, as the joy one directs towards those one must favour. Pavanar follows Parimelazhagar. The emphatic ஏ in தீதே underlines the surprising verdict that the pleasant fault is worse than the violent one.

tamil:
பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை அறிவினை
நிச்ச நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு.
transliteration:
Pochchaappuk kollum pukazhai arivinai
Nichcha nirappuk kon raangu.
current_meaning: Just as being poor day after day slowly destroys a person’s mind, being careless and forgetful destroys a person’s good name.
elementary: If a child is hungry every single day, it is very hard for them to think clearly at school. In the same way, if someone keeps forgetting their promises and jobs, people slowly stop trusting and admiring them, until their good name is gone.
university: The verb கொல்லும் (‘kills’) does strong work in both halves: பொச்சாப்பு kills புகழ் (fame) just as நிச்ச நிரப்பு kills அறிவு (understanding). Parimelazhagar glosses நிச்ச நிரப்பு as filling one's belly every day by begging. When this happens to a learned man, the humiliation and sin involved bring contempt on him and destroy the regard he enjoyed. In the same way, forgetfulness in a man of fame brings contempt, because he fails to guard himself and his affairs fall apart, and so it destroys his standing. Pavanar notes that நிரப்பு (literally ‘fullness’) is an auspicious euphemism for poverty, and he cross-refers to Kural 1046, where even the sound words of the poor go unheeded. Manakkudavar reads this couplet as part of a set on holding firm in worldly affairs. Parimelazhagar groups 531-532 as the couplets that state the fault of heedlessness. Editions split the final words either as நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு or as நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு; the sense is the same.
